new definition: Request for Proposal: a formal document asking suppliers to submit detailed offers.
old example: The RFP response was submitted before the deadline, with each requirement addressed in the correct section and a compliance matrix included at the back.
new example: We received the RFP on Monday and the deadline is Friday.

old definition: Service Level Agreement. The part of a contract that defines the performance standards a supplier must meet — such as uptime, response times, and what happens if those standards are not met.
new definition: Service Level Agreement: the part of a contract that sets the performance standards a supplier must meet.
old example: The SLA committed to 99.9% uptime and a four-hour response time for critical issues, with financial penalties applied if either target was missed.
new example: The SLA guarantees 99.9% uptime and a fast response to critical issues.

old definition: A company that sells products or services to another business. In formal procurement, all vendors are assessed and approved before they can be contracted.
new definition: A company that supplies goods or services to another business.
old example: Every vendor goes through a formal assessment before being approved to supply the organisation — covering financial stability, security posture, and compliance.
new example: We are pleased to be your preferred vendor for this project.

old definition: The right to officially approve a purchase. In most companies, different people hold sign-off authority depending on the value of the contract.
new definition: The official power to approve a purchase or contract.
old example: For contracts above a set value, only one senior person in the organisation holds sign-off authority — and the deal cannot proceed without their approval.
new example: Only one director has sign-off authority for a contract of this size.

word: HAS THIS GONE TO PROCUREMENT YET?
old definition: A way to ask if the deal has moved into the formal procurement stage. It helps you understand where you are in the process and what needs to happen next.
new definition: A question asking whether the deal has reached the formal buying department.
old example: Before planning next steps, it is worth asking: has this gone to procurement yet — or is the business team still completing their internal evaluation?
new example: Has this gone to procurement yet, or is it still with the business team?

word: THE PROPOSAL ADDRESSES EACH OF YOUR STATED REQUIREMENTS
old definition: A phrase you use to confirm that your proposal responds to every point the client listed. It shows you read their requirements carefully and answered them in order.
new definition: A statement confirming that the proposal responds to every requirement the client listed.
old example: The proposal addresses each of your stated requirements in sequence, with a compliance matrix at the back so your procurement team can verify the match point by point.
new example: The proposal addresses each of your stated requirements, from security to reporting.

word: ONCE BOTH PARTIES HAVE SIGNED THE CONTRACT
old definition: A phrase that refers to the moment the deal is legally finalised. It is used to describe what happens after signature — such as the start of implementation or the first invoice.
new definition: A phrase describing what happens after the deal is legally finalised by both sides.
old example: Once both parties have signed the contract, the implementation team will begin onboarding within five business days and the first project milestone will be set for week six.
new example: Once both parties have signed the contract, our team will begin implementation.

word: WHO ARE THE KEY STAKEHOLDERS WE SHOULD BE ENGAGING AT THIS STAGE?
old definition: A question you ask to find out which people need to be involved in the decision at a specific point in the process. It helps you avoid surprises later.
new definition: A question asking which people need to be involved in the decision right now.
old example: As the evaluation moves forward, it's important to ask: who are the key stakeholders we should be engaging at this stage — so no one is left out of the process at the final approval step.
new example: Who are the key stakeholders we should be engaging at this stage?

word: WE TYPICALLY SEE LEGAL REVIEW TAKE TWO TO THREE WEEKS — I'D FACTOR THAT INTO THE TIMELINE
old definition: A phrase used to warn the client that legal review takes time. It helps both sides plan the deal timeline so no one is surprised by delays near the close.
new definition: A warning that legal review usually takes about two to three weeks, so planning should allow for it.
old example: When planning the route to signature, it is worth noting that we typically see legal review take two to three weeks — I'd factor that into the timeline before confirming the board submission date.
new example: We typically see legal review take two to three weeks, so I'd factor that into the timeline.

old definition: A phrase used to explain that a specific part of your response is driven by the formal requirements in the RFP. It shows the buyer that you are following their process exactly.
new definition: A phrase explaining that part of your response follows a formal requirement in the RFP.
old example: The RFP requires us to address data residency and security in a dedicated section — the full response and supporting documentation start on page 22.
new example: The RFP requires us to provide a separate security section, so it is included.

old definition: In complex deals, a commitment is a specific, time-bound agreement to take a defined action — not a general expression of interest. 'We're interested in moving forward' is not a commitment. 'I will submit the proposal to procurement by Friday' is a commitment. Securing incremental commitments — small, specific agreements that build progressively toward contract — is the core discipline of complex deal management.
new definition: A specific agreement to take a defined action by a set date.
old example: Riley made the distinction explicit: Before we close today's meeting, I want to agree on a specific commitment from both sides — not a general intention, but a named action with a named owner and a date. My commitment is to send the mutual action plan by end of tomorrow. What is yours? — because 'we'll look at it this week' is the kind of commitment that turns into a three-week delay.
new example: Her commitment was to send the revised proposal to procurement by Friday.

old definition: The specific, named actions agreed at the end of every sales conversation — who does what, and by when. The absence of agreed next steps is the single most common cause of deal stall in complex B2B sales. A good set of next steps includes: the specific action, the named person responsible, and the exact date by which it will be completed.
new definition: The specific actions agreed at the end of a conversation, with owners and dates.
old example: Riley said: Before we finish — I want to make sure we have named next steps from today's conversation, not just a general plan to proceed. My experience is that 'we'll be in touch' is where deals go to die. So: you introduce me to Sarah by end of today, I send the mutual action plan by tomorrow morning, and we schedule a three-way check-in for Monday at 10 a.m. Can we confirm all three now?
new example: Let's confirm the next steps before we end today's meeting.

old definition: The sequence of events, approvals, and milestones that must occur before a complex purchase can be finalised — including internal reviews, sign-off stages, board presentations, and legal processes. Understanding the full decision timeline — and mapping it explicitly — is the first step in managing a complex close. Without it, both parties are working to unstated and potentially conflicting assumptions about when and how the deal will close.
new definition: The sequence of approvals and milestones a buyer must complete before purchasing.
old example: Riley said: Let's make the decision timeline explicit — not as a pressure tool, but because both our teams need to plan around it. Walk me through every step that has to happen on your side from today to signed contract. Once we have the full picture, I can map our side against it and identify where the pinch points are likely to be.
new example: Could you walk me through your decision timeline from here to signature?

old definition: An internal advocate within the buyer's organisation who actively supports the vendor's solution and helps navigate internal decision-making on the vendor's behalf. A champion is distinct from a sponsor — a sponsor has authority; a champion has access and willingness to advocate. The most effective complex deal closures rely on an internal champion who has visibility across all approval stages and can surface issues before they become blockers.
new definition: A person inside the buyer's company who supports your solution and advocates for it.
old example: Riley asked directly: Who inside your organisation is the champion for this deal — the person who, when I'm not in the room, is making the case for why this is the right decision? That person doesn't have to be the most senior stakeholder — they just need visibility, credibility, and a genuine belief in the value of the solution. Because without a champion, deals at this level tend to get deprioritised the moment something else competes for internal attention.
new example: Our champion in finance has helped us move through every approval stage.

old definition: A shared document — agreed by both buyer and seller — that maps every step required from both sides to close the deal, with a named owner and a specific date assigned to each action. A mutual action plan (MAP) is one of the most effective tools in complex deal management: it creates shared accountability, surfaces gaps in the process, and provides a visual reference that both teams can refer to independently.
new definition: A shared document listing every action, owner and date needed to close a deal.
old example: Riley proposed the MAP: Can I suggest we formalise this as a mutual action plan — a shared document that maps every step from today to signed contract, with a named owner and a specific date for each action? I'll draft it on my side and send it to you by end of tomorrow. Once you've reviewed and added your team's actions, it becomes the reference document for both teams. Nothing moves without it being in the plan, and anything that falls behind is immediately visible.
new example: I'll send the mutual action plan to your team by tomorrow morning.

old definition: Any factor — technical, commercial, organisational, or political — that is preventing a deal from advancing. Blockers can be explicit (a stakeholder with an unresolved objection) or hidden (an internal policy the vendor doesn't know about, a competing initiative, a stakeholder who has not been engaged). Surfacing blockers early — through direct questioning — is significantly more effective than discovering them when the deal has already stalled.
new definition: Any factor that prevents a deal from moving forward.
old example: Riley asked with deliberate directness: I want to ask a question you might find unusual: what are the blockers we haven't discussed yet? Not the concerns we've addressed — I'm thinking about the things that might be creating hesitation internally that haven't surfaced in our conversations. In my experience, there is almost always at least one. I'd rather know now than find out six weeks from now when the timeline has slipped.
new example: Is there a blocker on your side that we haven't discussed yet?

old definition: An external factor or internal motivation that could cause a decision to be made faster than the standard process would suggest — a competitor win that creates urgency, a budget deadline, a strategic initiative that the solution directly supports, or an executive mandate. Identifying accelerators helps a salesperson understand what factors might compress the decision timeline — and allows them to reference those factors without manufacturing false urgency.
new definition: A factor that could make a buyer decide faster than usual.
old example: Riley asked: Is there anything that could accelerate the decision — something on your side that would make moving faster genuinely valuable for your organisation? Not from my perspective — I understand you have a process to follow. But sometimes there's a factor like a competitor who has already moved, a platform that's going end-of-life, or a strategic initiative where the timing matters. If something like that exists, I'd like to know, so we can factor it into the plan.
new example: Is there an accelerator, such as a budget deadline, that affects your timing?

old definition: A mandatory approval checkpoint in a buyer's internal process that must be cleared before the deal can advance to the next stage. Complex enterprise deals typically have multiple sign-off gates: procurement approval, IT security clearance, legal review, and C-suite or board sign-off. Missing or bypassing a sign-off gate is one of the most common deal-killing errors — often caused by the vendor not knowing the gate exists until the deal is already through it.
new definition: A required approval checkpoint that must be cleared before a deal can advance.
old example: Riley mapped the gates explicitly: Based on what you've described, I can see four sign-off gates between today and signed contract: procurement approval, IT security clearance, legal review, and CFO sign-off before the board. Are those the only four — or are there gates in the process I haven't accounted for? Because the timeline we've built depends on those four being the complete picture.
new example: Legal review is the last sign-off gate before the contract reaches the board.

word: WHAT DOES THE DECISION-MAKING PROCESS LOOK LIKE FROM HERE?
old definition: The phrase for mapping the full internal approval process at the point where a deal is close to advancing. It opens the conversation about every step that must happen before the contract can be signed — without creating pressure or implying a specific timeline. The answer typically reveals sign-off gates, stakeholders, and process requirements that the vendor did not previously know about.
new definition: Used to ask about every step in the buyer's internal approval process.
old example: Riley said after Marcus confirmed they were 'close': Before we talk about timing, I want to make sure I understand the decision-making process completely. What does the decision-making process look like from here — every step, every approval, every person who needs to be involved before this can be signed? I'd rather build a realistic timeline than an optimistic one that slips.
new example: We're nearly aligned, so what does the decision-making process look like from here?

word: CAN WE AGREE ON A MUTUAL ACTION PLAN — MAPPING EVERY STEP ON BOTH SIDES?
old definition: The phrase for proposing a mutual action plan as the mechanism for managing the close. Framing it as 'both sides' is deliberate — it signals that the seller is not imposing a process but proposing a shared accountability structure. The MAP typically becomes the reference document that both teams check against independently.
new definition: Used to propose a shared plan that lists every action on both sides.
old example: Riley proposed: Can we agree on a mutual action plan that maps every step from today to contract — with a named owner and a specific date for each action? I'll draft my side and send it to you by end of tomorrow. Once you've added your team's steps, we have a shared reference that makes the timeline visible and keeps both sides accountable.
new example: Can we agree on a mutual action plan, mapping every step on both sides?

word: WHAT WOULD NEED TO HAPPEN FOR US TO HAVE A SIGNED CONTRACT BY [DATE]?
old definition: The phrase for working backwards from a target close date to identify every action, approval, and milestone that must occur before that date. It is a collaborative question — it does not set the deadline, it asks the buyer to help identify what the deadline requires. This makes the buyer a partner in mapping the timeline rather than a subject of the seller's urgency.
new definition: Used to work backwards from a target date and identify the required steps.
old example: Riley asked: The board meeting is six weeks away — and that feels like our natural anchor point. What would need to happen for us to have a signed contract by the Thursday before that meeting? I want to map every single step between now and that date, assign owners, and build in enough buffer that a one-week delay in any stage doesn't kill the timeline.
new example: What would need to happen for us to have a signed contract by March 15?

word: WHO DO WE NEED TO BRING ALONG INTERNALLY ON YOUR SIDE BEFORE THIS CAN MOVE FORWARD?
old definition: The phrase for stakeholder mapping at the close — identifying any internal parties who have not yet been fully engaged and whose absence could block the deal at a later stage. 'Bring along' implies inclusion and alignment rather than pressure — it is collaborative language that invites the buyer to name their own internal blockers.
new definition: Used to ask which internal people must be included before the deal can progress.
old example: Riley said: I want to make sure we're not surprised by a stakeholder who hasn't been part of the conversation. Who do we need to bring along internally on your side before this can move forward — and what do they each need to be confident about? If there's a sceptic in the room, it's better to know now and address their concern directly.
new example: Who do we need to bring along internally on your side before this can move forward?

word: I WANT TO MAKE SURE WE HAVE A NAMED NEXT STEP FROM TODAY — NOT JUST A PLAN TO PROCEED
old definition: The phrase for ensuring that every sales conversation ends with a specific, committed next action — not a vague intention. The distinction between a plan to proceed and a named next step is the difference between momentum and stall. A named next step includes a specific action, a named person, and a specific date.
new definition: Used to ask for one clear, specific action to follow the conversation.
old example: Riley said as the call was wrapping up: Before we close — I want to make sure we have a named next step from today, not just a plan to proceed. The specific actions: you introduce me to Sarah today, I send the mutual action plan by end of tomorrow, and we schedule the three-way check-in for Monday at 10. Does that work, or do we need to adjust any of the three?
new example: I want to make sure we have a named next step from today, not just a plan to proceed.

word: IS THERE A BUDGET CYCLE OR BOARD APPROVAL PROCESS WE SHOULD BE PLANNING AROUND?
old definition: The phrase for identifying external drivers that constrain or accelerate the decision timeline — particularly budget cycles, board meeting dates, or contract expiry dates that create natural urgency. These are legitimate urgency drivers that the seller can reference without manufacturing false pressure.
new definition: Used to ask about financial or approval deadlines that affect the decision timing.
old example: Riley asked early in the closing conversation: Is there a budget cycle or board approval process we should be planning around? Not because I'm trying to create urgency from my side — but because these timelines often have real consequences if they're missed. If there's a quarterly board meeting where this would be presented, or a budget that needs to be committed before year-end, that shapes the entire plan.
new example: Is there a budget cycle or board approval process we should be planning around?

old definition: A short summary of what was discussed and agreed in a previous conversation. A good recap also reminds the buyer of the key points and confirms what happens next.
new definition: A short summary of what was discussed and agreed in an earlier conversation.
old example: A good recap should bridge what was raised in the meeting to what was agreed — and clearly flag the one open question both sides still need to resolve.
new example: I'll send a quick recap of the three options we mapped out today.

old definition: A message that reconnects the buyer to the reason they were interested in the first place. It reminds them of the problem they wanted to solve and why the solution matters.
new definition: A message that reminds the buyer why they wanted the solution in the first place.
old example: A well-timed value reminder reconnects the buyer to the specific outcome they came for — not the product, but the conversion improvement they originally said they wanted.
new example: My value reminder showed how the new funnel could lift your conversions by thirty-five percent.

old definition: Information or materials you prepare to help the buyer get approval inside their organisation. It gives them what they need to explain the decision to others when you are not in the room.
new definition: Materials prepared to help a buyer win approval inside their own organisation.
old example: Good decision support gives the buyer a document with the ROI figures, the risk provisions, and the key commercial terms — so they can walk into the board meeting fully prepared.
new example: Here is the decision support folder, with the figures your leadership team will ask about.

old definition: Getting back in contact with a buyer who has gone quiet. The best reengagement gives them a specific reason to respond — not just a general check-in.
new definition: The act of getting back in touch with a buyer who has gone quiet.
old example: Effective reengagement gives the buyer a specific reason to respond — a new client result or a relevant industry development — not a generic check-in message.
new example: My reengagement email mentioned the new case study, and she replied within an hour.

old definition: Building relationships with more than one person inside the buyer's organisation. This protects the deal if your main contact becomes unavailable or loses influence.
new definition: Building relationships with several people inside the buyer's company, not just one contact.
old example: Multi-threading means building relationships across procurement, IT, and finance — so the deal doesn't stall if one contact goes quiet or loses influence.
new example: Through multi-threading, we now have allies in IT, operations, and finance.

old definition: How fast deals move through your sales process. When deals slow down or get stuck, pipeline velocity drops and targets become harder to reach.
new definition: The speed at which deals move through the stages of your sales process.
old example: A deal stuck at the same stage for three weeks drags down pipeline velocity — finding the specific blocker at that stage is the first step to moving it forward.
new example: Our pipeline velocity has slowed because three deals are stuck waiting on legal review.

old definition: Any planned contact with a buyer — a call, email, meeting, or message. The best touch points add value to the buyer's decision, not just remind them you exist.
new definition: Any planned moment of contact with a buyer, such as a call or meeting.
old example: Each touch point in a follow-up sequence should move the deal forward — a call, a document, or a meeting — with something the buyer didn't have before.
new example: Our next touch point is a call on Thursday, then a meeting in person.

old definition: Anything that makes a deal less likely to close. Common risks include a key contact going quiet, a budget freeze, or a competitor gaining access to the account.
new definition: Anything that makes it less likely that a deal will close.
old example: Deal risk can come from several directions at once — a budget freeze, a key contact leaving, a market shift, or a blocker inside the buying organisation — and recognising which one is active early makes the difference.
new example: The budget freeze is our biggest deal risk on this account right now.

word: FOLLOWING OUR CONVERSATION ON [DATE], I WANTED TO SEND A BRIEF RECAP
old definition: A phrase used to open a follow-up message. It connects the email to a specific previous conversation and shows the recap is short and purposeful.
new definition: A polite opening line for a short email that summarises an earlier conversation.
old example: Following our conversation on Tuesday, I wanted to send a brief recap of what we covered, what we aligned on, and the one open question we still need to resolve before moving forward.
new example: Following our conversation on Monday, I wanted to send a brief recap of the next steps.

word: I'M NOT REACHING OUT TO PUSH — I WANT TO OFFER SUPPORT WITH WHATEVER YOU'RE WORKING THROUGH INTERNALLY
old definition: A phrase that tells the buyer you are calling to help, not to pressure them. It positions you as a resource, not a problem.
new definition: A phrase that tells the buyer you want to help, not pressure them.
old example: I'm not reaching out to push — I wanted to share a document, a reference contact, and a cost summary that might help you navigate the approval process from the inside.
new example: I'm not reaching out to push, I want to offer support with whatever you're working through internally.

word: BASED ON WHAT YOU SHARED LAST TIME, THE MOST RELEVANT THING I CAN OFFER RIGHT NOW IS
old definition: A phrase that shows you remembered what the buyer told you and are connecting it to something specific and relevant now.
new definition: A phrase that links what the buyer told you earlier to something useful you can offer now.
old example: Based on what you shared last time about pressure on delivery timelines, I've put together the performance data that speaks directly to that challenge — the results are from a comparable organisation in your sector.
new example: Based on what you shared last time, the most relevant thing I can offer right now is this downtime analysis.

word: I'VE PUT TOGETHER A ONE-PAGE SUMMARY FOR YOUR [CFO/BOARD/TEAM] — HAPPY TO TALK THROUGH IT BEFORE YOU SHARE IT
old definition: A phrase used to offer a short, focused document the buyer can use in their internal conversations. Offering to review it together first gives both sides a chance to align before it is shared.
new definition: A phrase offering a short document for the buyer's colleagues, with a chance to review it together first.
old example: I've put together a one-page summary with the key return figures, the risk provisions, and the implementation timeline — one document your team can take straight into the decision conversation.
new example: I've put together a one-page summary for your board, happy to talk through it before you share it.

word: SINCE WE LAST SPOKE, [SOMETHING RELEVANT HAS CHANGED] — I THOUGHT THAT WAS WORTH SHARING
old definition: A phrase used to introduce new information as a reason to reconnect. The update should be genuinely relevant to what the buyer cares about.
new definition: A phrase that introduces a relevant update as a natural reason to get back in touch.
old example: Since we last spoke, a client who faced the same challenge completed their rollout and saw strong results in the exact metric they'd flagged as their biggest concern — I thought it was worth sharing before your next review.
new example: Since we last spoke, our results have improved noticeably, and I thought that was worth sharing.

word: I DON'T WANT TO LOSE MOMENTUM — CAN WE AGREE ON WHAT THE RIGHT NEXT TOUCH POINT LOOKS LIKE?
old definition: A phrase used to agree on a clear next step before the conversation ends. It keeps the deal moving instead of letting it drift back into silence.
new definition: A phrase used to agree on a clear next step so the deal keeps moving.
old example: I don't want to lose momentum — can we agree on a specific next step now, whether that's a call, a document review, or a demo, along with a date and what each side will have ready?
new example: I don't want to lose momentum, can we agree on what the right next touch point looks like?

old definition: The boundaries of what a project includes — and what it does not include. Clear scope protects both the vendor and the buyer from disagreements later.
new definition: The limits of what a project includes and what it leaves out.
old example: The scope of the engagement covers platform configuration, CRM integration, and onboarding — custom development and data migration are explicitly excluded.
new example: The scope covers configuration and onboarding, but not custom development.

old definition: A specific output the vendor agrees to produce by a set point in the project. A proposal lists deliverables so both sides know exactly what will exist at the end of each phase.
new definition: A specific item that a vendor agrees to produce by a set date.
old example: The key deliverable at the end of phase two is a fully configured platform, tested against all technical requirements and ready for the first wave of users.
new example: The main deliverable for this phase is a fully tested dashboard.

old definition: A key point in a project timeline that marks the end of a phase. Each milestone is usually tied to a specific deliverable and a payment instalment.
new definition: An important point in a project timeline that marks the end of a phase.
old example: The project has four milestones — each one triggers a formal sign-off and the corresponding payment instalment before the next phase begins.
new example: We reach the second milestone in week ten, after the platform review.

old definition: Inputs or actions that must come from the buyer or a third party before the vendor can complete a milestone. If a dependency is delayed, the project timeline adjusts accordingly.
new definition: Things the client or a third party must provide before the work can continue.
old example: The week-three integration milestone has three dependencies on the buyer's side: API credentials within five business days, a nominated IT lead by week two, and sandbox access.
new example: Our timeline has three dependencies, starting with your team's access credentials.

old definition: The conditions a proposal is built on. If an assumption turns out to be wrong after the contract is signed, the scope or cost may need to change.
new definition: Conditions that are accepted as true when a proposal is prepared.
old example: This proposal is built on two key assumptions — a standard CRM configuration and a user group of no more than 50 people — and both need to be confirmed before signature.
new example: Our assumptions include a user group of fifty and a standard configuration.

old definition: Items or services that are not included in the scope of a proposal. Stating exclusions clearly prevents the buyer from assuming something is covered when it is not.
new definition: Things that are specifically not included in a proposal or its price.
old example: The exclusions in this proposal cover custom development, multilingual content, and legacy data migration — all three are out of scope at the quoted price.
new example: The exclusions are custom development, translation work, and legacy data migration.

old definition: The financial and legal conditions of a contract — including price, payment schedule, termination rights, and SLA provisions. They are usually presented last, after value and scope have already been established.
new definition: The price, payment schedule, and legal conditions of a contract.
old example: The commercial terms set out a total of £420,000 payable in four milestone-linked instalments, with net 30 payment terms, a mutual termination right after month six, and financial penalties for missed SLA targets.
new example: Our commercial terms include four instalments and payment within thirty days.

old definition: A formal process for managing any changes to scope, timeline, or cost after a contract is signed. Both sides must approve in writing before any change is made or any additional cost is incurred.
new definition: A formal process for approving any change to a signed contract.
old example: Every change to the agreed scope goes through a change control process — no work begins and no additional invoice is raised without written approval from both sides.
new example: Under change control, every request needs written approval before any extra work starts.

word: I'D LIKE TO WALK YOU THROUGH THE PROPOSAL SECTION BY SECTION
old definition: A standard opening for a proposal presentation. It signals that the presenter will guide the client through each section one by one, rather than leaving them to read and interpret the document alone.
new definition: A phrase used to begin explaining a document one part at a time.
old example: I'd like to walk you through the proposal section by section — pausing for questions after each one — so we're aligned on intent before we reach the commercial terms.
new example: I'd like to walk you through the proposal section by section, starting with the objectives.

word: THE SCOPE OF THIS ENGAGEMENT INCLUDES [X] — AND I WANT TO BE EQUALLY CLEAR ABOUT WHAT IT DOES NOT INCLUDE
old definition: A phrase for presenting scope with clear, explicit boundaries. The second half is as important as the first — it prevents the most common source of post-contract misunderstanding.
new definition: A phrase used to state clearly what a project covers and what it does not.
old example: The scope of this engagement includes platform configuration, CRM integration, and onboarding for up to 50 users — and I want to be equally clear about what it does not include: custom development, multilingual content, and third-party data sources outside the standard library.
new example: The scope of this engagement includes configuration for fifty users, and I want to be equally clear about what it does not include.

word: THE KEY DELIVERABLE AT THIS MILESTONE IS
old definition: A phrase for linking a specific output to a point on the project timeline. It makes accountability measurable — both sides know exactly what must exist before the milestone can be signed off.
new definition: A phrase used to name the main item the vendor will produce at a project stage.
old example: The key deliverable at this milestone is a fully configured and tested platform environment — validated against all technical requirements, formally signed off, and triggering the next payment instalment.
new example: The key deliverable at this milestone is a tested platform, ready for your approval.

word: THE PRICING IS STRUCTURED AS [X] — LET ME EXPLAIN WHAT'S INCLUDED AND HOW WE ARRIVED AT THAT FIGURE
old definition: A phrase for presenting pricing with transparency and confidence. It frames the total as the logical result of the scope already described — broken down into what each component covers and how the figure was calculated.
new definition: A phrase used to introduce a price and explain how it was calculated.
old example: The pricing is structured as four milestone-linked instalments — let me explain what's included in each and how we arrived at the overall figure: the platform licence and approximately 1,200 hours of dedicated implementation resource.
new example: The pricing is structured as four instalments, so let me explain what's included and how we arrived at that figure.

word: THIS PROPOSAL IS BASED ON A SET OF ASSUMPTIONS — IF ANY OF THESE CHANGE, WE'D NEED TO REVISIT THE SCOPE AND COST
old definition: A phrase for naming proposal assumptions transparently before the contract is signed. It protects the vendor if conditions change, and gives the buyer a clear opportunity to correct anything that is wrong.
new definition: A phrase used to warn that the price and scope depend on certain conditions.
old example: This proposal is based on a set of assumptions — a standard CRM configuration and a user group of no more than 50 — and if any of these change before signature, we'd need to revisit the scope and cost.
new example: This proposal is based on a set of assumptions, and if any of these change, we'd need to revisit the scope and cost.

word: I'D WELCOME ANY QUESTIONS ON THE COMMERCIAL TERMS BEFORE WE MOVE TO NEXT STEPS
old definition: A closing phrase for the commercial terms section. 'Welcome' signals confidence — it invites scrutiny rather than hoping the terms are accepted without question. Moving to 'next steps' keeps the conversation moving toward agreement.
new definition: A phrase used to invite questions about price and contract conditions before continuing.
old example: I'd welcome any questions on the commercial terms before we move to next steps — on pricing, payment timing, or termination rights — so we can address any concerns now rather than after the document goes to legal.
new example: I'd welcome any questions on the commercial terms before we move to next steps.

old definition: The revenue target a salesperson is expected to hit in a given period. It is set by the sales manager and used to measure individual performance.
new definition: The sales target a salesperson must reach in a given period.
old example: The team finished the quarter at 115% of quota — every rep exceeded their individual target, with the top performer closing 15% above their assigned number.
new example: Our team finished the quarter at 115% of quota.

old definition: The percentage of quota a salesperson or team has achieved in a given period. It shows how close they are to hitting their target.
new definition: The percentage of a sales target that has been achieved so far.
old example: At 58% attainment at the mid-point of the quarter, the team needed to accelerate three key deals to close the gap before quarter-end.
new example: We're sitting at 58% attainment with half the quarter gone.

old definition: Regular one-to-one sessions between a sales manager and a rep to develop skills, review deals, and improve performance through questioning and reflection rather than giving direct answers.
new definition: Regular guidance from a manager to help a salesperson improve their skills.
old example: Weekly coaching sessions helped identify a gap in the rep's discovery process and led to faster deal progression and stronger close rates by the following month.
new example: Our weekly coaching sessions helped me spot gaps in my discovery calls.

old definition: The ratio of total pipeline value to quota. It shows whether a rep or team has enough active deals to hit their target for the period.
new definition: The ratio of the value of open deals to the sales target.
old example: Pipeline coverage had dropped to 2.1:1 — well below the minimum needed to close the quarter with confidence, so new opportunities had to be added immediately.
new example: Pipeline coverage has fallen from 3.8 to 2.1 times our target.

old definition: A prediction of how much revenue the team will close in a given period. It is split by confidence level — commit, best case, and upside.
new definition: A prediction of how much revenue the team will close in a period.
old example: The forecast showed $52M committed, but six deals flagged as at risk meant the actual close number was likely to fall short of that figure.
new example: The forecast shows 52 million, but six deals look shaky.

old definition: Any factor that makes a deal less likely to close on time or at the expected value — such as no agreed next step, stalled activity, or missing stakeholders.
new definition: Anything that makes a deal less likely to close on time.
old example: The deal had been in the same stage for 47 days with no agreed next step and several key stakeholders not yet engaged — all clear signs of deal risk.
new example: This deal has been stuck for 47 days, which is a serious deal risk.

old definition: The period of time it takes a new salesperson to reach full quota. During ramp, quota expectations are reduced to reflect the learning curve.
new definition: The period when a new salesperson builds up to a full sales target.
old example: New reps typically take four months to ramp — expectations start at 10% of quota in month one and increase each month as skills and pipeline develop.
new example: During ramp, new reps start at ten percent of quota.

old definition: The percentage of deals a salesperson wins out of the total number they compete for. It is a key measure of sales effectiveness and deal quality.
new definition: The percentage of competitive deals that a salesperson or team actually wins.
old example: A drop in win-rate from 38% to 24% prompted a review of the late-stage sales process to identify where and why deals were being lost to competitors.
new example: Our win rate fell from 38% to 24% this year.

word: WALK ME THROUGH WHERE THIS DEAL IS — NOT THE PITCH, TELL ME WHERE THE DEAL ACTUALLY IS
old definition: A phrase a sales manager uses to get an honest, fact-based update on a deal. It signals they want the real position — last activity, agreed next step, stakeholder gaps — not an optimistic version.
new definition: A manager's request for an honest, factual update on the real status of a deal.
old example: Walk me through where this deal is — not the pitch, tell me where the deal actually is: last meaningful meeting, agreed next step, and who still has not been engaged.
new example: Walk me through where this deal is, not the pitch, tell me where the deal actually is.

word: WHAT'S YOUR PLAN TO CLOSE THIS BEFORE QUARTER END?
old definition: A coaching question that challenges a rep to explain their specific closing plan. It moves the conversation from optimism to concrete, dated actions with named stakeholders.
new definition: A question asking a salesperson to explain exactly how they will win a deal by the deadline.
old example: What's your plan to close this before quarter-end — who are you meeting, in what order, and what needs to happen at each step to reach a signature by the deadline?
new example: What's your plan to close this before quarter end? Show me each step and date.

word: WHAT WOULD YOU DO DIFFERENTLY IF YOU COULD GO BACK TO THE FIRST CALL?
old definition: A coaching question that helps a rep reflect on what they would change. It builds learning from a stalling deal without the manager prescribing the answer.
new definition: A question inviting a salesperson to reflect on what they would change about a deal.
old example: What would you do differently if you could go back to the first call — would you have qualified the decision process earlier, or engaged more stakeholders from the start?
new example: What would you do differently if you could go back to the first call?

word: I'M GOING TO COMMIT [X] TO THE FORECAST — WHAT ARE YOU COMMITTING?
old definition: A phrase a sales manager uses when asking each rep to name the revenue they are certain they will close. It creates shared accountability for the team forecast.
new definition: A manager's way of asking each salesperson to name the revenue they are sure to close.
old example: I'm going to commit $7.3M to the forecast — what are you committing? Give me the number you will stand behind, not your best-case pipeline figure.
new example: I'm going to commit 7.3 million to the forecast, what are you committing?

word: THE STRATEGY FOR Q3 IS [X] — EVERY REP SHOULD BE ABLE TO EXPLAIN THEIR PERSONAL VERSION IN 60 SECONDS
old definition: A phrase a sales leader uses to cascade strategy and require every rep to personalise it. It confirms understanding by asking each person to connect the direction to their own territory and accounts.
new definition: A leader's way of asking each salesperson to explain the team strategy in their own terms.
old example: The strategy for Q3 is enterprise expansion — every rep should be able to explain their personal version in 60 seconds: which accounts, what the opportunity is, and what they are doing differently this quarter to activate it.
new example: The strategy for Q3 is enterprise expansion, and every rep should be able to explain their personal version in 60 seconds.

word: I WANT TO HEAR YOUR THINKING — TELL ME WHAT YOU SEE AND WHAT YOU'D DO
old definition: A coaching phrase a manager uses to hear the rep's own analysis first. It develops independent thinking by putting the rep in the lead before the manager gives any input.
new definition: A manager's way of asking a salesperson to share their own analysis and plan first.
old example: I want to hear your thinking — tell me what you see and what you'd do: walk me through the deal, identify what's working and what's not, and give me your recommendation before I give you mine.
new example: I want to hear your thinking, tell me what you see and what you'd do.

old definition: A potential customer who has shown some interest but has not yet been checked to see if they are a real sales opportunity. Not every lead becomes a deal.
new definition: A person or company that might buy from you but has not been checked yet.
old example: The salesperson added 12 new leads to the CRM after a week of outreach and inbound enquiries.
new example: She is not sure if this lead is worth a call.

old definition: All the deals a salesperson is currently working on, at different stages of the sales process. A healthy pipeline has deals at many stages — not all near the close.
new definition: All the deals a salesperson is working on at different stages.
old example: The salesperson has nine active deals in the pipeline at different stages.
new example: Our pipeline looks strong, with deals at every stage this month.

old definition: A specific sales opportunity with a named customer. Each deal has a value, a stage, a close date, and an owner. To close a deal means to win it.
new definition: A possible sale to a named customer, with a value and a stage.
old example: The biggest deal in the pipeline is worth $28,000 and is currently in the negotiation stage.
new example: He moved the deal to stage two and added the value.

old definition: A record of what was discussed with a customer, saved in the CRM after every call or meeting. Good notes mean any colleague can continue a deal without asking you for information.
new definition: A short written record of a call or meeting, saved in the CRM.
old example: The salesperson logged a note after the call with a summary, the agreed terms, and the next step.
new example: She wrote a note about the renewal before closing the client file.

old definition: The current stage of a deal in the pipeline — for example 'proposal sent', 'negotiating', or 'closed won'. Always keep statuses up to date so your manager can forecast accurately.
new definition: The stage a deal has reached in the sales process.
old example: The status of the deal was updated to 'negotiation' after the revised proposal was sent.
new example: He changed the status to MVP build after the team meeting.

old definition: To check if a lead is a real sales opportunity — do they have the budget, authority, need, and right timeline? Qualifying leads early saves time.
new definition: To check if a lead is a good fit and worth following up.
old example: The salesperson qualifies every lead within 48 hours to decide if they are worth spending time on.
new example: She will qualify each lead by company size and budget.

old definition: To record a call, email, or meeting in the CRM. Logging keeps the CRM accurate and means the whole team has a shared picture of every customer relationship.
new definition: To write down a call, email or meeting in the CRM.
old example: The salesperson logs every call the same day with a summary, agreed next step, and follow-up date.
new example: He needs to log this call before he leaves the office.

old definition: An estimate of how much revenue the salesperson expects to earn this quarter, based on the deals in the pipeline and how likely they are to close.
new definition: An estimate of the sales you expect to make in a period.
old example: The salesperson's forecast for the quarter is around $80,000, based on four deals that are likely to close.
new example: Our forecast shows revenue reaching the target by the first quarter.

old definition: The standard question in a pipeline review for asking about a specific deal. The answer should include the stage, recent activity, and next step.
new definition: A question you ask to find out the current stage of a deal.
old example: The manager asked 'What's the status of the Brightfield deal?' and the salesperson explained it was at negotiation stage.
new example: What's the status of the deal with the logistics client?

old definition: The standard phrase for reporting that you recorded an interaction in the CRM. Always say when you logged it to confirm the CRM is up to date.
new definition: A phrase you use to say you recorded a call or meeting in the CRM.
old example: The salesperson said 'I logged a note after the call on Tuesday with a summary of everything we agreed.'
new example: I logged a note after the call, with the next steps for Ms. Mokoena.

word: I HAVE [X] DEALS IN MY PIPELINE AT [STAGE]
old definition: The standard way to report your pipeline in a review. Always include the number of deals and the stage. Say 'in my pipeline' — never 'on my pipeline'.
new definition: A phrase you use to say how many deals you have at a given stage.
old example: The salesperson reported 'I have nine deals in my pipeline — three at proposal stage and two in negotiation.'
new example: I have four deals in my pipeline at proposal stage.

old definition: A phrase for reporting how you categorised a deal in the CRM — using a status label or a probability percentage.
new definition: A phrase you use to say what status or chance of closing you gave a deal.
old example: The salesperson said 'I've marked the Brightfield deal as 90% probability with a close date of Friday.'
new example: I've marked it as 70% probability, so it should close this month.

word: ANYONE SHOULD BE ABLE TO PICK UP THE DEAL WITHOUT CALLING ME
old definition: The standard for good CRM notes — if your notes are complete, any colleague can continue a deal without contacting you. Used by managers to set the expectation for note quality.
new definition: A sentence meaning your notes are so clear that a colleague can continue the deal alone.
old example: The manager said good CRM notes mean anyone should be able to pick up the deal without calling you.
new example: My notes are complete, so anyone should be able to pick up the deal without calling me.

word: WHAT DOES YOUR FORECAST LOOK LIKE FOR THIS QUARTER?
old definition: The standard question about expected revenue in a pipeline review. The answer should include the number of deals expected to close and their total value.
new definition: A question asking how much you expect to sell in the current quarter.
old example: The manager asked 'What does your forecast look like?' and the salesperson said four deals would close for around $80,000.
new example: What does your forecast look like for this quarter?

old definition: Any moment when a customer comes into contact with your brand — an ad, a website visit, an email, or a phone call. Every touchpoint is a chance to make a good impression.
new definition: A moment when a customer comes into contact with a brand.
old example: The team identified eleven touchpoints in the customer journey from the first ad to the signed contract.
new example: Every email is a touchpoint, so we should map each one.

old definition: The first stage of the customer journey — when the customer discovers your brand for the first time. The customer is not ready to buy yet; they are just learning you exist.
new definition: The stage when a customer first learns that a brand exists.
old example: About 12,000 people reach the awareness stage each month through search and social media ads.
new example: He stopped when the sign caught his eye, and awareness began.

old definition: The stage where the customer knows about your brand and is comparing you to other options — reading reviews, watching demos, and asking questions.
new definition: The stage when a customer compares different options before deciding what to buy.
old example: At the consideration stage, customers want to compare products and read case studies before making a decision.
new example: She is in the consideration stage and reads reviews for each pair.

old definition: The moment a customer takes the action you want — buying, signing up, or becoming a paying customer. The conversion rate is the percentage of people who take that action.
new definition: The moment a customer takes the action you want, such as buying.
old example: The conversion rate from free trial to paid customer is 18%, which is below the industry average.
new example: He tapped the button, and the conversion was complete.

old definition: Keeping customers after they have bought — making sure they stay and do not leave for a competitor. Retention is often cheaper than finding new customers.
new definition: Keeping customers so they continue to buy from you over time.
old example: The 12-month retention rate is 74%, meaning 26% of customers leave within the first year.
new example: Our loyalty card helps retention, and regular customers love it.

old definition: A model that shows how many people move from one stage of the journey to the next. It is wide at the top (many people) and narrow at the bottom (fewer buyers).
new definition: A model showing how many people move from one stage to the next.
old example: The team found that the biggest drop in the funnel happens between the awareness and consideration stages.
new example: Most people leave at the top of the funnel.

old definition: A realistic profile of a typical customer — including their job, goals, and how they make decisions. A persona helps the team create content that speaks to a specific type of customer.
new definition: A made-up profile of a typical customer, with goals and needs.
old example: The team created three personas to make sure the journey map was relevant to each type of customer.
new example: This persona cares about financial security and protecting his home.

old definition: The point in the customer journey where people stop and do not continue to the next stage. A drop-off means something is not working at that point.
new definition: The point where customers stop and do not continue to the next stage.
old example: The biggest drop-off is between the free trial and the paid subscription — 82% of trial users do not convert.
new example: There is a big drop-off right in the middle of the journey.

old definition: The standard way to describe what a customer is thinking or doing at each point in the journey. Always name the stage and then describe the customer's behaviour.
new definition: A phrase used to describe what a customer thinks or does at a journey stage.
old example: At the awareness stage, the customer has just discovered the brand and is curious but not ready to buy.
new example: At the comparison stage, the customer looks at other options.

word: THE CUSTOMER FIRST ENCOUNTERS THE BRAND WHEN...
old definition: A phrase for describing the very first touchpoint in the journey — the moment a customer first comes into contact with your brand. Always follow it with a specific channel or action.
new definition: A phrase used to describe the first time a customer meets a brand.
old example: The customer first encounters the brand when they see a LinkedIn ad targeting marketing managers.
new example: The customer first encounters the brand when she sees a message on her phone.

old definition: A phrase for identifying where customers stop progressing in the funnel. Always follow it with a specific stage or moment, then ask why.
new definition: A phrase used to show the exact point where customers stop moving forward.
old example: The biggest drop-off happens at day seven of the free trial, when most inactive users stop engaging.
new example: The drop-off happens at the payment step, when the progress bar stalls.

word: WE NEED TO IMPROVE THE EXPERIENCE AT...
old definition: A phrase for recommending action on a specific part of the customer journey. Always name the specific stage or touchpoint — not a vague description.
new definition: A phrase used to say which part of the journey needs work.
old example: The team agreed they need to improve the experience at the post-demo follow-up and the day-seven onboarding check-in.
new example: We need to improve the experience at this point, right here on the map.

old definition: A phrase for setting a clear purpose for every customer interaction. Use it when designing or reviewing a journey map to make sure every touchpoint does something useful.
new definition: A phrase used to say what purpose each customer contact should have.
old example: The manager said each touchpoint should either build awareness, move the customer closer to a decision, or strengthen their confidence.
new example: Each touchpoint should have one clear goal.

word: THE GOAL AT THIS STAGE IS TO...
old definition: A phrase for stating the marketing objective at a specific point in the funnel. The goal is different at each stage — awareness, consideration, conversion, and retention each need a different approach.
new definition: A phrase used to state the aim for a particular step in the journey.
old example: The goal at the consideration stage is to give customers enough information to choose the product over a competitor.
new example: The goal at this stage is to help buyers feel ready to choose.

old definition: The first words you say when you start a call. A professional greeting includes your name and your company.
new definition: The first words you say when you start a call.
old example: Riley started the call with a clear greeting: Good morning, this is Riley from Practispeak Solutions. It told Marcus exactly who was calling before he said anything.
new example: The customer liked her friendly greeting on the phone.

old definition: To say your name and company at the start of a call. You introduce yourself so the customer knows who is calling and why.
new definition: To tell someone your name and who you are.
old example: Riley said: Let me introduce myself — my name is Riley and I work for Practispeak Solutions. We spoke at the conference last month.
new example: Let me introduce myself, I am Riley from Brightline sales.

old definition: The reason for your call. Always state your purpose clearly and early — customers do not like to guess why someone is calling.
new definition: The reason why you do something, like making a call.
old example: Riley explained her purpose in one sentence: The reason I am calling is to follow up on the proposal I sent you last week. Short, clear, professional.
new example: The purpose of my call is to understand your challenges.

old definition: A good time for someone — when they are not busy and can talk. Always check if the time is convenient before you start your call.
new definition: Good or easy for you, like a time when you are free.
old example: Before Riley started explaining, she asked: Is now convenient for you? Marcus said: Yes, I have a few minutes. Go ahead.
new example: Is this a convenient time to talk about the offer?

old definition: In a short amount of time — not too long. When you say you will be brief, you show you respect the customer's time.
new definition: In a short way, using only a few words or a little time.
old example: Marcus was busy, so Riley said: I will be brief — this will only take two minutes. I just want to check if you have any questions about the proposal.
new example: I will explain the new offer briefly.

old definition: To contact someone again after a first conversation or meeting. In sales, you follow up to keep the conversation moving forward.
new definition: To contact someone again after you spoke or met before.
old example: Riley said: The reason I am calling is to follow up on our last meeting. I wanted to check if you had any questions about the plan.
new example: I am calling to follow up on the proposal.

old definition: A recorded message you leave when someone does not answer the phone. A good voicemail is short and includes a reason to call back.
new definition: A recorded message you leave when nobody answers the phone.
old example: Marcus did not answer, so Riley left a voicemail: Hi Marcus, this is Riley from Practispeak. Please call me back when you are free — I have some good news about your proposal.
new example: I left a voicemail for the customer this morning.

old definition: Free to talk or meet at a particular time. When you call, you check if the customer is available before you start.
new definition: Free and able to talk or help at this time.
old example: Riley asked: Are you available to talk for a few minutes? Marcus said: Yes, I am free now. Riley said: Perfect — I will be brief.
new example: Yes, I am available to talk with you now.

old definition: The standard professional opening for a business call. Always say your name and company first — never assume the customer knows who you are.
new definition: A common way to start a business call and say who you are.
old example: Riley called Marcus and said: Good morning, this is Riley from Practispeak Solutions. That one sentence told Marcus who was calling and where they worked.
new example: Good morning, this is Anna from Brightline.

old definition: Use this to confirm you have the right person before explaining your reason for calling. 'Speaking with' is the professional standard — not 'talking to'.
new definition: A polite question to check that you have the right person.
old example: Riley heard someone answer the phone. She said: Am I speaking with Marcus Oliveira? He said: Yes, speaking. Riley said: Great — good morning, Marcus.
new example: Hello, am I speaking with Mr. Brown?

word: THE REASON I AM CALLING IS
old definition: A clear, direct way to state your purpose. Say this early in the call — customers want to know why you are calling within the first thirty seconds.
new definition: A clear way to say why you are calling.
old example: Riley got straight to the point: The reason I am calling is to follow up on the proposal I sent last week. I wanted to see if you had any questions.
new example: The reason I am calling is your new order.

old definition: Check if the customer can talk before you start. It shows you respect their time and gives them a chance to ask you to call back later.
new definition: A polite question to ask if the person can talk now.
old example: Before Riley started her call, she asked: Is now a good time to talk for a few minutes? Marcus said: Yes, go ahead. Riley said: Great — I will be brief.
new example: Hello Mr. Brown, is now a good time?

old definition: A polite, natural way to end a call. It tells the customer the conversation is finishing without being rude or abrupt.
new definition: A polite way to say that the call is ending.
old example: Riley had everything she needed. She said: I will let you go now — thank you for your time, Marcus. I will send the details by email today.
new example: Thank you for your time, I will let you go.

word: I WILL FOLLOW UP BY EMAIL
old definition: Tell the customer what happens next after the call. It shows you are organised and gives them something to expect from you.
new definition: A way to say you will send an email after the call.
old example: Marcus was not ready to decide. Riley said: No problem at all — I will follow up by email with all the details. Take your time and let me know if you have questions.
new example: I will follow up by email tomorrow morning.

old definition: To welcome someone at the start of a conversation. A professional greeting includes your name, your company, and a check that you have the right person.
new definition: To welcome someone when you first meet or speak to them.
old example: Riley called a new customer and started with a clear greeting: Good morning — my name is Riley from Practispeak Solutions. Am I speaking with Marcus Oliveira?
new example: I always greet every customer with a smile.

old definition: To present yourself or a product for the first time. After greeting, you introduce the reason for your call and the product you want to talk about.
new definition: To show or present something or someone for the first time.
old example: Riley said: Let me introduce our Standard Plan — it is designed for sales teams of ten to twenty people and includes reporting tools, priority support, and unlimited storage.
new example: Let me introduce our new product to you.

old definition: To point out the most important or attractive feature of a product. When you highlight something, you draw the customer's attention to the part that matters most to them.
new definition: To show the most important or best part of something.
old example: Riley said: I want to highlight the reporting feature — your manager will love it. It gives you real-time data on every deal in your pipeline, automatically.
new example: I want to highlight the main feature of this plan.

old definition: A reason a customer gives for not buying yet — for example, the price is too high or they need more time. Objections are normal — a good salesperson listens and responds calmly.
new definition: A reason a customer gives for not wanting to buy.
old example: Marcus said: It sounds good, but can I think about it? Riley recognised it as an objection and said: Of course. Let me give you a quick summary of everything first.
new example: The price is a common objection.

old definition: The order of steps in a process. A sales call has a clear structure: greeting → product → price → close. Following the structure makes you sound organised and professional.
new definition: The order and way the parts of something are put together.
old example: Before the call, Riley thought about the structure: start with a warm greeting, introduce the product, explain the price clearly, and finish with a confident close.
new example: A sales call has a simple structure.

old definition: Feeling sure of yourself and your message. A confident salesperson speaks clearly, answers questions directly, and does not apologise for the price.
new definition: Sure about yourself and what you are saying.
old example: Marcus asked about the price. Riley answered confidently: The price is $35 per user per month. For your team of fifteen, that is $525. It is one of the best values in the market.
new example: She sounds confident when she talks about the price.

old definition: A short statement that repeats the most important points. Always give a summary before you close — it reminds the customer what they are getting and removes any last doubts.
new definition: A short talk or text that gives the main points again.
old example: Before Marcus gave his final answer, Riley said: Let me give you a quick summary — the Standard Plan, fifteen users, $35 per month, with 10% off for the first three months. Does that sound right?
new example: Here is a short summary of the offer.

old definition: To complete a sale — the moment the customer says yes. The close comes after you have answered all questions and given a summary. A simple, direct question is always best.
new definition: To finish a sale when the customer says yes.
old example: Riley had answered every question. She gave the summary and then closed the sale: Wonderful — would you like to go ahead? Marcus said: Yes — let's do it.
new example: She smiled and said, "Let's close the sale today."

word: GOOD MORNING — MY NAME IS [NAME] FROM [COMPANY]
old definition: The standard opening for a professional sales call. Say your full name and company clearly — never assume the customer knows who you are.
new definition: A polite way to start a work call or meeting with a new person.
old example: Riley started the call: Good morning — my name is Riley from Practispeak Solutions. Am I speaking with Marcus Oliveira? That single sentence told Marcus exactly who was calling and where they worked.
new example: Good morning, my name is Sam from Brightline.

word: I WOULD LIKE TO TELL YOU ABOUT [PRODUCT]
old definition: The phrase that moves you from the greeting to the product. 'Tell you about' is the natural way to introduce a product — 'say you about' is a common mistake.
new definition: A way to start talking about a product with a customer.
old example: Riley confirmed she had the right person. She then said: I would like to tell you about our Standard Plan — it is designed for sales teams of ten to twenty people and I think it is perfect for your team.
new example: I would like to tell you about our Standard Plan.

old definition: A direct, confident way to state the price. Do not apologise for it or say 'unfortunately'. State it clearly, then immediately connect it to the customer's situation.
new definition: A way to say how much a product costs for each user or month.
old example: Marcus asked how much the plan cost. Riley said: The price is $35 per user per month. For your team of fifteen, your total would be $525 per month — less than $3 per person per day.
new example: The price is $35 per user per month.

word: LET ME GIVE YOU A QUICK SUMMARY
old definition: Say this before you ask for the close. It repeats the key details — product, users, price, offer — so the customer can confirm everything is right before they say yes.
new definition: A polite way to say you will repeat the main points in a short way.
old example: Marcus said he was almost ready to decide. Riley said: Let me give you a quick summary first — the Standard Plan, fifteen users, $35 per month, with 10% off for three months. Does that sound right?
new example: Let me give you a quick summary of the offer.

old definition: Use this when a customer gives an objection or says they need more time. It shows you are listening and want to understand — not just push them to say yes.
new definition: A question to ask what worries the customer most.
old example: Marcus said he needed to think about it. Riley did not panic. She said: Of course — what is your main concern? Is it the price, the features, or something else? I am happy to help.
new example: What is your main concern about the plan?

word: WOULD YOU LIKE TO GO AHEAD?
old definition: The closing question — simple, direct, and confident. After the summary, this is all you need to say. Do not over-explain. Ask the question and wait for the answer.
new definition: A question to ask if the customer wants to start and buy.
old example: Riley finished the summary and paused. Then she asked: So — would you like to go ahead? Marcus smiled and said: Yes — let's do it. I am ready to start.
new example: Would you like to go ahead with the order?

old definition: To say that something is a good choice for someone. When you recommend something, you give your professional opinion — not just information.
new definition: To say that something is a good choice for someone.
old example: I recommend the Standard Plan for your team.
new example: I recommend the Pro plan for your team.

old definition: To give someone an idea or option to think about. Similar to recommend, but a little softer — you are offering an idea, not making a strong decision.
new definition: To give someone an idea to think about.
old example: Can I suggest the Basic Plan? It is a good place to start.
new example: Can I suggest the Basic Plan for your team?

old definition: One of the things you can choose from. When you have two or more things to pick from, each one is an option.
new definition: One thing you can choose from a group of things.
old example: The Basic Plan is a good option for small teams.
new example: This is a good option for city driving.

old definition: Right for what someone needs. If something is suitable, it fits the situation — it is not too much, not too little.
new definition: Right for what a person needs.
old example: The Basic Plan is suitable for a small team.
new example: The Basic Plan is suitable for a small team.

old definition: To fit with what someone needs. When a product matches a customer's needs, it is the right product for them.
new definition: To fit what someone needs or wants.
old example: The Standard Plan is a good match for a team of five.
new example: This plan can match your budget.

old definition: The best possible choice for a specific situation. Similar to perfect, but often used when you are explaining why something is the best fit.
new definition: The best choice for a certain person or situation.
old example: The Basic Plan is ideal for new customers.
new example: The Basic Plan is ideal for new customers.

old definition: The decision you make when you pick one thing from several options. You can also say a good choice when you want to tell a customer they have decided well.
new definition: The thing you pick when you can choose from several things.
old example: The Standard Plan is a good choice for your team.
new example: The Standard Plan is a good choice for your team.

old definition: The most direct way to make a recommendation. Clear, professional, and confident — you are giving your opinion as a salesperson, not just showing options.
new definition: A direct way to say which option you think is best.
old example: I recommend this one. It is easy to use and not expensive.
new example: I recommend this one for your small team.

word: THIS IS A GOOD FIT FOR YOU
old definition: A friendly way to say a product matches the customer's needs. It sounds personal — you are connecting the product to this specific customer, not just describing it.
new definition: A friendly way to say a product is right for the customer.
old example: This is a good fit for you. It covers everything you need.
new example: I think this is a good fit for you.

old definition: A soft way to suggest something new. You are not saying the customer is wrong — you are opening a door to a different option they may not have considered.
new definition: A polite way to suggest a new idea to someone.
old example: Have you thought about the Standard Plan? It has more features.
new example: Have you thought about the Standard Plan?

word: BASED ON WHAT YOU TOLD ME
old definition: A phrase that shows you listened to the customer. Before you make a recommendation, you connect it to something they said — this makes the recommendation feel personal and well-reasoned.
new definition: A phrase that shows you used the customer's own words to decide.
old example: Based on what you told me, the Standard Plan is the best option.
new example: Based on what you told me, the Standard Plan fits best.

old definition: A way to explain why a product suits a specific person or situation. Instead of just saying it is good, you say who it is good for.
new definition: A phrase to say who or what a product is good for.
old example: This would work well for a team your size.
new example: This would work well for a team your size.

word: MOST OF OUR CUSTOMERS IN YOUR SITUATION CHOOSE
old definition: A phrase that uses social proof — you are telling the customer that others like them have already made this choice. It is reassuring and helps customers feel more confident in their decision.
new definition: A phrase that tells a customer that people like them pick this option.
old example: Most of our customers in your situation choose the Standard Plan.
new example: Most of our customers in your situation choose the Standard Plan.

old definition: A number that a customer gives to show how happy they are — for example, 1 to 5 stars.
new definition: A number that shows how happy a customer is.
old example: Our average rating on G2 is 4.7 out of 5 — one of the highest in our category.
new example: Our rating is 4.7 out of 5 stars.

old definition: A written comment from a customer about their experience with a product or service.
new definition: A written comment from a customer about a product or service.
old example: A new client said they found us through a review on G2 — positive reviews really help.
new example: One client wrote a very nice review about our support.

old definition: A positive statement from a happy customer, used in marketing to show others the product works.
new definition: A kind statement from a happy customer about a product or service.
old example: We use client testimonials on our website — real words from real people are more convincing than ads.
new example: We put a customer testimonial on our website.

old definition: A score that shows how likely customers are to recommend your product to someone else. Often called NPS.
new definition: A score that shows how likely customers are to recommend a company.
old example: Our NPS is 72 — a score above 50 is considered excellent in the B2B sector.
new example: Our net promoter score went up this quarter.

old definition: Contact a customer again after a complaint or feedback to check if the issue was resolved.
new definition: To contact someone again to check on something from before.
old example: We always follow up on complaints within 24 hours to make sure the client is happy.
new example: I'm calling to follow up on your complaint from Monday.

old definition: Change one thing into something else — for example, turn a complaint into an opportunity.
new definition: To change one thing into something else.
old example: We turned a complaint into a case study — the client had a problem, we fixed it, and they became one of our best advocates.
new example: We can turn this complaint into a chance to help.

old definition: Request a customer's opinion about their experience.
new definition: To ask a customer for their opinion about a product or service.
old example: We ask for feedback at the end of every project — most clients are happy to share their thoughts.
new example: We ask for feedback after every delivery.

old definition: Manage and respond to an unhappy customer in a professional way.
new definition: To deal with a customer who is unhappy about something.
old example: The key to handling a complaint well is to listen, acknowledge the problem, and fix it quickly.
new example: Our team can handle a complaint in one day.

old definition: Write a public comment on a platform about a product or service.
new definition: To write a public comment online about a product or service.
old example: We ask happy clients to leave a review on G2 — it helps new customers decide to sign up.
new example: Could you leave a review on our website?

old definition: Easy to change or adapt to different needs.
new definition: Easy to change for different needs.
old example: It is a flexible contract — you can switch from monthly to annual at any time.
new example: This modular sofa is very flexible for any office.

old definition: Set to happen automatically at a fixed time or on a regular basis.
new definition: Planned to happen at a fixed time.
old example: A scheduled report goes out every Friday so your team starts the weekend with the latest numbers.
new example: Your scheduled report arrives every Monday at nine.

old definition: A screen that shows real-time information and updates automatically.
new definition: A screen that shows new information as it happens.
old example: You get a live dashboard — you can see every deal and every customer in one place, right now.
new example: You can use a live dashboard for your team.
