old definition: A thorough document or summary with full information and data.
new definition: A document with a lot of information and numbers.
old example: I can show you a detailed report — it breaks down performance by team member, by week, and by deal size.
new example: I prepared a detailed report for your team.

old definition: An agreement that can be changed or adapted to fit the customer's needs.
new definition: An agreement that is easy to change.
old example: It is a flexible contract — monthly or annual, and you can change at any time.
new example: This is a flexible contract with monthly billing.

old definition: A product or service built specifically around a customer's exact requirements.
new definition: A product made just for one customer's needs.
old example: For larger teams, we offer a custom solution — it is built around your exact workflow and tools.
new example: I can offer you a custom solution for your team.

old definition: A function that is already included in the product with no extra setup.
new definition: A part that is already inside the product.
old example: The integration with your email tool is a built-in feature — it connects automatically when you sign up.
new example: The water dispenser is a built-in feature.

old definition: A report the system creates and sends on its own, on a schedule you set.
new definition: A report that the system makes and sends by itself.
old example: You can set up an automated report — choose the day and time, and it goes out without you doing anything.
new example: This is an automated report for your sales team.

old definition: A question that digs deeper than the first answer to find the real cause.
new definition: Aimed at digging deeper than a first answer to find the real cause.
old example: Her probing questions moved the conversation from the surface issue to the real reason behind the delay.
new example: Her probing questions took us from the symptoms to the real cause.

old definition: A question that checks you have understood exactly what someone means.
new definition: Meant to check that you have understood exactly what someone means.
old example: He asked a clarifying question to find out which car size she actually had in mind.
new example: She asked a clarifying question about which type of car he preferred.

old definition: A likely result or consequence that follows from a situation or decision.
new definition: A likely result or consequence that follows from a situation or decision.
old example: The main implication of these delays is that our biggest clients may lose trust in us.
new example: The main implication of this delay is that clients may lose trust.

old definition: An idea that might be true but has not yet been confirmed.
new definition: An idea that might be true but has not yet been confirmed.
old example: My hypothesis is that the new campaign will lift sales, but we need to test it.
new example: My hypothesis is that the new process will raise sales, but we need data.

old definition: A method of questioning that begins with broad questions and narrows to specific ones.
new definition: A questioning method that starts with broad questions and narrows to specific ones.
old example: I used a funnel approach, starting with your goals and ending with the one issue slowing you down.
new example: I used a funnel to move from your goals to the one problem.

word: I'D LIKE TO CHALLENGE THAT ASSUMPTION GENTLY — HAVE YOU CONSIDERED...?
old definition: A gentle way to question someone's belief and suggest another possibility.
new definition: A polite way to question someone's belief and suggest another possibility.
old example: I'd like to challenge that assumption gently: have you considered that the board may prefer the other approach?
new example: I'd like to challenge that assumption gently: have you considered the board's view?

word: IF THAT'S THE CASE, WHAT DOES THAT MEAN FOR...?
old definition: A question asking what the result will be if a situation stays the same.
new definition: A question asking what the result will be if a situation continues.
old example: If that's the case, what does that mean for your team's workload and your service ratings?
new example: If that's the case, what does that mean for your team's workload?

old definition: To present the same situation from a different angle, changing how it is perceived without changing the facts. Reframing is not spin — it is helping the prospect see what they already know from a more useful perspective.
new definition: To present a situation from a different angle to change how people see it.
old example: Marcus said the cost was too high. Riley reframed it: not as a cost, but as the price of not fixing a problem that was already costing him far more. The number did not change — what changed was the context around it.
new example: Let me reframe the price as an investment in your team.

old definition: To explicitly acknowledge that a concern is real and understandable before addressing it. Skipping validation makes objections worse — the prospect feels dismissed and digs in deeper.
new definition: To show that you accept someone's concern as real and understandable.
old example: Riley did not argue with Marcus when he said the timing was wrong. She validated it first: 'That makes complete sense given where you are in the quarter.' Only then did she ask what would need to change for the timing to work.
new example: I want to validate your concern about the implementation timeline.

old definition: To delay a decision or postpone an action to a later point. In sales, a prospect who defers may have a genuine timing constraint — or may be using timing as a polite way to say no. Distinguishing between the two is one of the most important skills in objection handling.
new definition: To delay a decision until a later time.
old example: Marcus deferred twice in the same meeting — first on budget, then on timing. Riley's job was to find out whether he was genuinely waiting for the right moment or whether he had already decided and was being polite about it.
new example: The client decided to defer the purchase until next quarter.

old definition: A real limitation — financial, structural, or time-based — that restricts what a prospect can do. Understanding whether a constraint is fixed or flexible is the first step in responding to almost any objection.
new definition: A limit that restricts what someone is able to do.
old example: The budget constraint Marcus described was real — but it was a constraint on the current quarter, not on the year. Riley asked about the annual cycle and discovered that the budget she needed would be available in six weeks.
new example: Budget is the main constraint for the client this quarter.

old definition: To address an objection before the prospect raises it — removing it from the conversation before it becomes a barrier. Experienced salespeople preempt the objections they know are coming rather than waiting to be ambushed by them.
new definition: To deal with a problem before anyone has raised it.
old example: Riley knew the trust objection was coming — the industry had been burned by failed implementations before. She preempted it in her opening: 'I want to address something before we get to the proposal, because I know it is on your mind.'
new example: I wanted to preempt any concerns about the delivery schedule.

old definition: The level of investment — financial, time, or reputational — that a prospect is being asked to make. Many objections are not about the specific objection raised but about the commitment feeling too large or too risky for where the relationship currently is.
new definition: A promise or obligation to invest money, time, or effort.
old example: Marcus's hesitation was not really about money. It was about commitment — he was being asked to sign a twelve-month contract with a company he had only met twice. Riley proposed a pilot, which reduced the commitment to something he could defend internally.
new example: A twelve-month contract felt like too big a commitment to the client.

old definition: Doubt about whether something is true, effective, or worth trusting. Trust objections are fundamentally rooted in scepticism — often built up by previous experiences with other vendors or with the category itself.
new definition: A feeling of doubt about whether something is true or trustworthy.
old example: Marcus's scepticism was earned: his last two vendors had made similar promises and delivered disappointing results. Riley did not try to talk him out of the scepticism — she acknowledged it, used it to ask better questions, and offered to prove her claims on his own data.
new example: The buyer met our claims with a healthy dose of scepticism.

old definition: To involve a more senior person in a decision — either from the prospect's side (a decision-maker who needs to approve) or from your own side (a senior stakeholder who adds credibility). Authority objections often require a structured escalation to move forward.
new definition: To pass a matter to a more senior person.
old example: When Marcus said he would need to bring this to his CEO, Riley did not see it as a setback. She asked who else would be in that conversation and offered to help Marcus prepare for it — turning the escalation into a collaborative next step rather than a delay.
new example: I will escalate this request to our regional director today.

old definition: Validate the objection in full, then pivot — without using 'but', which signals that what came before did not count. 'And' keeps both things true at the same time.
new definition: A phrase that accepts the customer's concern, then continues without saying 'but'.
old example: I hear that the budget is not there for this quarter — and I want to make sure that when Q1 opens up, you have everything you need to make the case internally. Can we use this time to build that?'
new example: I hear that, and I'd like to show you our pilot results.

word: HELP ME UNDERSTAND WHAT'S BEHIND THAT
old definition: A probe that goes beneath the surface objection — because the stated reason and the real reason are often different. Used when you suspect the objection is a proxy for something deeper.
new definition: A request asking someone to explain the real reason for their objection.
old example: 'Help me understand what's behind the timing concern — is it that Q4 is genuinely the wrong moment, or is there something about the proposal itself that is making you want to wait?'
new example: Help me understand what's behind that before we discuss the proposal.

old definition: A conditional test — removes the stated objection hypothetically to discover whether it is the real barrier or a proxy for something else. If removing the issue does not change the answer, the real objection is elsewhere.
new definition: A phrase asking what the customer would decide if one concern disappeared.
old example: 'If the budget were not an issue right now — if you had the money approved and ready — would this be the right decision for your team?' If the answer is no, the real conversation is just beginning.
new example: If that weren't an issue, would you be ready to sign today?

word: WHO ELSE NEEDS TO BE PART OF THIS
old definition: The clean way to surface an authority gap without embarrassing the person you are speaking to. Frames the question as a process question, not a challenge to their decision-making power.
new definition: A question asking which other people must be involved in the decision.
old example: 'Who else needs to be part of this conversation before we move to next steps? I want to make sure the right people have everything they need.'
new example: Who else needs to be part of this discussion?

old definition: A forward-looking probe for timing objections — asks what conditions would need to be different for this to make sense. Moves the conversation from 'not now' to 'what would make now possible.'
new definition: A question asking which conditions must be different for the customer to say yes.
old example: 'What would need to change between now and Q1 for this to be the right moment? I want to understand what you are waiting for — so I can either help create those conditions or adjust what I am proposing.'
new example: What would need to change for you to approve the proposal?

word: THE COST OF NOT ACTING IS
old definition: Reframes a budget or timing objection by making the price of inaction visible. More effective than defending the cost of acting — because the prospect already knows what they are being asked to spend.
new definition: A phrase that highlights the price of doing nothing.
old example: 'The cost of not acting on this before year-end is roughly the same as the contract value — you lose twelve months of compounding efficiency gains and your competitor, who started in January, gains six months on you. I want to make sure that trade-off is visible.'
new example: The cost of not acting is losing market share to your competitors.

old definition: A level in a structured set of options — each pricing tier typically offers more features, capacity, or support than the one below it.
new definition: A level in a set of options, each with different features or prices.
old example: Brightline has three tiers — Basic, Standard, and Premium. Each one is designed for a different stage of team growth.
new example: The Premium tier includes a dedicated account manager.

old definition: A bundle of features, services, or products offered together at a set price — everything that comes with a particular plan.
new definition: A set of products or services sold together at one price.
old example: The Standard package includes the pipeline dashboard, automated follow-up reminders, and onboarding support — everything most growing teams need.
new example: The Standard package includes onboarding and automated follow-up reminders.

old definition: To move to a higher tier or plan — to switch to a package that includes more features, users, or capacity.
new definition: To move to a higher plan that offers more features or users.
old example: You could start with Standard and upgrade to Premium once the team has adopted the core tool and you are ready for the advanced reporting layer.
new example: You can upgrade to Premium at any time.

old definition: Able to grow with the customer's needs — a scalable plan adjusts as the team expands without requiring a complete switch.
new definition: Able to grow or change as your needs get bigger.
old example: The Standard plan is scalable — it supports up to twenty-five users, so you have room to grow without needing to move to a different tier immediately.
new example: The Standard plan is scalable for teams of up to twenty-five users.

old definition: A limit on usage within a plan — a maximum number of users, actions, or features allowed before you need to upgrade.
new definition: A limit on how much of something you can use.
old example: The Basic plan has a cap of five users — once your team grows beyond that, you would automatically need to move to Standard.
new example: The Basic plan has a cap of five users.

old definition: A group of features or services packaged together as a unit — often at a better price than buying each one separately.
new definition: A group of products or services sold together.
old example: The Premium bundle includes everything in Standard plus advanced analytics, custom reporting, and a dedicated account manager.
new example: The Premium bundle includes advanced analytics and a dedicated account manager.

old definition: Able to be adjusted to suit different situations or needs — a flexible plan can be modified, scaled, or cancelled without major disruption.
new definition: Easy to change to fit different needs.
old example: All plans are monthly and flexible — you are not locked into anything, which means you can adjust as your team's needs change.
new example: Our monthly plans are very flexible.

old definition: The process of setting up and getting started with a product — often guided by the vendor, and included in higher-tier plans.
new definition: The process of helping a new customer start using a product.
old example: The Standard plan includes dedicated onboarding — a setup session with our team to make sure everything is configured correctly before your reps go live.
new example: The Standard plan includes a dedicated onboarding session.

old definition: Introduce what the entry-level tier covers — sets the baseline before explaining what the higher tiers add.
new definition: Used to start describing what the lowest-priced plan offers.
old example: The Basic plan includes the core pipeline dashboard for up to five users — it is designed for small teams or those who want to try the tool before committing to more.
new example: The Basic plan includes the pipeline dashboard for up to five users.

word: THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO IS
old definition: Explain clearly what separates one tier from another — helps the prospect understand what they would gain or lose by choosing one over the other.
new definition: Used to explain how two options are not the same.
old example: The difference between Standard and Premium is the reporting layer — Standard gives you the pipeline view, Premium adds custom analytics and a dedicated account manager.
new example: The difference between the two is the reporting.

old definition: Signal when a higher tier would be appropriate — frames upgrading as a response to genuine need, not a sales move.
new definition: Used to say that a bigger plan is useful when you want extra features.
old example: If you need more than twenty-five users or want the advanced reporting features, that is when Premium starts to make sense.
new example: If you need more users, Premium is the better fit.

word: MOST TEAMS AT YOUR STAGE GO WITH
old definition: Use social proof to guide the prospect toward the most suitable plan — shows that the recommendation is based on experience with similar teams, not just a sales preference.
new definition: Used to say that similar companies usually choose a certain plan.
old example: Most teams at your stage — twelve reps, growing fast, first time using a structured pipeline tool — go with Standard. It gives you everything you need without overcomplicating the rollout.
new example: Most teams at your stage go with Standard.

word: YOU COULD ALWAYS START WITH AND UPGRADE LATER
old definition: Lower the commitment threshold — present upgrading as easy, natural, and low-risk so the prospect does not feel locked in.
new definition: Used to say a customer can begin with one plan and move up later.
old example: You could always start with Standard and upgrade to Premium later once you have seen the value and the team is ready for more. There is no penalty for upgrading mid-cycle.
new example: You could always start with Standard and upgrade later.

old definition: Explain concretely what a particular plan or feature delivers — translates a tier name or feature list into a real outcome.
new definition: Used to explain the real benefit of a plan or feature.
old example: The Standard plan — what that gets you is full pipeline visibility for the whole team, automated follow-up reminders, and onboarding support so you are not setting it up alone.
new example: What that gets you is full pipeline visibility for the whole team.

old definition: How your brand sits in the minds of your target audience — what it stands for and how it compares to alternatives.
new definition: The place your brand holds in customers' minds compared with others.
old example: Our positioning is 'the affordable premium option' — we sit between the budget players and the luxury brands, which is exactly where our audience wants us.
new example: Our positioning is affordable premium, between budget and luxury brands.

old definition: What makes your brand genuinely different from competitors — the specific thing that gives people a reason to choose you.
new definition: The special quality that makes your brand different from others.
old example: Our differentiation is speed — we guarantee campaign results in 30 days, which no competitor is willing to promise.
new example: Our differentiation is speed, and no other agency promises results in 30 days.

old definition: The advantage your brand has over competitors — the thing that makes you harder to replace.
new definition: A special advantage that puts you ahead of other companies.
old example: Our competitive edge is our data. We have three years of first-party campaign data across 200 B2B clients — no agency our size can match that.
new example: Our competitive edge is three years of campaign data from 200 clients.

old definition: The full range of products, services, or past work a company offers or has done — used to show capability and experience.
new definition: A collection of a company's products, services, or past work.
old example: Before the pitch, send the client your portfolio — three or four case studies that show results in their industry are worth more than any slide deck.
new example: I will send the client our portfolio before the pitch tomorrow.

old definition: The clear statement of what you offer, who it is for, and why it is valuable — the core of your marketing message.
new definition: A clear statement of what you offer and why it is valuable.
old example: Your value proposition needs to answer one question in under ten seconds: why should I choose you over everyone else?
new example: Our proposition is simple: an integrated platform with dedicated support for your hotel.

old definition: The specific group of people or companies you are trying to reach and sell to — defined by industry, role, size, or behaviour.
new definition: The group of people or companies you want to sell to.
old example: Our target market is not 'all B2B companies' — it is SaaS companies with 50–500 employees who are scaling their sales team for the first time.
new example: Our target market is small software companies that are hiring their first sales team.

old definition: How well your target audience knows your brand exists and what it stands for — the foundation before any sales conversation can happen.
new definition: How well people know that your brand exists.
old example: We had a great product but zero brand awareness — no one had heard of us. The first six months were entirely focused on getting our name in front of the right people.
new example: We had a great product, but our brand awareness was very low.

old definition: How well a marketing activity or partnership aligns with your brand's overall goals and direction.
new definition: How well something matches your company's goals and direction.
old example: Before saying yes to a co-marketing opportunity, always ask: is this a strategic fit? Does it reach our audience, reinforce our positioning, and help us grow in the right direction?
new example: This partnership has a strong strategic fit with our audience and our brand.

old definition: To be clearly different and more noticeable than other brands in your space — in a way that matters to your audience.
new definition: To be clearly different from other companies and easy to notice.
old example: In a crowded SaaS market, you do not stand out by having more features — you stand out by being clearer about who you are for and why you exist.
new example: We need a bold new message to stand out from the competition.

old definition: To define a very specific position in the market that you own — rather than trying to appeal to everyone.
new definition: To create a small, specific place in the market for yourself.
old example: We carved out a niche in B2B LinkedIn marketing for tech companies — it feels narrow, but it is where we win every time.
new example: We want to carve out a niche in LinkedIn marketing for tech firms.

old definition: To successfully enter a new market — especially one that is competitive or where you have no existing presence.
new definition: To successfully enter a new and difficult market.
old example: Breaking into the enterprise market took us two years — our positioning was wrong at first and we had to rebuild from scratch.
new example: It took us two years to break into the enterprise market.

old definition: To use your existing advantages as the foundation for your marketing strategy — rather than trying to fix every weakness first.
new definition: To use what you already do well as a base for growth.
old example: The brief told us to build on their client retention rate — 94% is exceptional, and we made it the centrepiece of every piece of content.
new example: Our campaign will build on your strengths, starting with your high client retention.

old definition: To actively demonstrate what makes you different — through your messaging, proof, and positioning.
new definition: To show clearly that you are different from other companies.
old example: What sets us apart is not just what we do — it is how we do it. No lock-in contracts, weekly reporting, and a dedicated account manager from day one.
new example: Weekly reports and a dedicated manager set us apart from other agencies.

old definition: To make sure a specific marketing activity connects to and supports the bigger strategic goal.
new definition: To make sure an activity supports your larger plan.
old example: Before approving any campaign, ask: does this align with the strategy? If it does not move us towards our positioning goal, it is a distraction.
new example: Every new campaign must align with our brand strategy.

old definition: Relating to how people think, what they value, and what motivates them — not just who they are on paper.
new definition: Relating to people's values, interests, attitudes, and how they think.
old example: Demographic data tells us our buyer is a 38-year-old marketing director. Psychographic data tells us she values speed over perfection, distrusts jargon, and makes decisions based on peer recommendations.
new example: Our psychographic data shows that buyers value speed over perfection.

old definition: Relating to what people actually do — how they search, buy, engage, and respond — rather than what they say they do.
new definition: Relating to what people actually do, such as how they search and buy.
old example: Behavioural segmentation showed us that our best clients always download a case study before booking a call — so we put case studies at the front of every campaign.
new example: Behavioural data shows that most visitors download a case study first.

old definition: The specific problem or desire that is driving someone to look for a solution right now — the emotional and practical context behind a purchase.
new definition: The situation and feeling that makes someone look for a solution right now.
old example: The need-state for our best clients is not 'I want better marketing' — it is 'I need to justify my budget to the board in 90 days and I am running out of time'.
new example: Her need-state is urgent, because she has a deadline and no time.

old definition: A detailed profile of a fictional but realistic customer — built from real data and used to guide every marketing and sales decision.
new definition: A detailed imaginary customer based on real data about your buyers.
old example: We created three personas for the campaign — but 80% of our best clients matched just one of them, so we rebuilt the whole strategy around her.
new example: Most of our best clients match this one persona.

old definition: A summary of who a customer segment is — their role, industry, company size, goals, and challenges.
new definition: A short description of a customer group, such as their job and goals.
old example: The ideal customer profile for TechFlow is an operations director at a manufacturing company with 100–500 employees who has recently been given a cost-reduction target.
new example: The ideal customer profile is an operations director at a mid-sized factory.

old definition: Basic factual information about a person or group — age, gender, job title, company size, location, and industry.
new definition: Basic facts about a group of people, such as age, job, and location.
old example: The demographic is a useful starting point, but it is the psychographic layer — what they care about and how they make decisions — that makes the marketing actually work.
new example: The demographic for this campaign is managers aged thirty to forty-five.

old definition: A distinct group within a larger audience that shares specific characteristics — and can therefore be reached with the same message.
new definition: A smaller group within a larger audience that shares similar features.
old example: We split the database into three segments: active clients, lapsed clients, and cold prospects. Each got a completely different email — same brand, three different conversations.
new example: We sent a different email to each segment of the database.

old definition: A specific problem or frustration that a customer experiences — and that your product or service solves.
new definition: A specific problem that regularly frustrates a customer.
old example: The number one pain point for our persona is wasted marketing budget with no proof of results. Every piece of content we create addresses that directly.
new example: Wasted budget is the biggest pain point for our persona.

old definition: To focus very specifically on one segment rather than a broad group — getting precise about who exactly you are talking to.
new definition: To focus closely on one particular group of people.
old example: Once we zeroed in on operations directors with a cost-reduction brief, our click-through rate tripled — the content finally felt written for them, not everyone.
new example: We decided to zero in on operations directors for this campaign.

old definition: To address a specific customer problem directly in your marketing — in a way that shows you understand it.
new definition: To talk directly about a customer's problem in your message.
old example: The ad that performed best spoke directly to the pain point: 'Still waiting for your marketing agency to show you the ROI?' — it doubled our click-through rate overnight.
new example: This ad speaks to the pain point of slow reporting.

old definition: To connect with an audience at an emotional or practical level — to say something that feels personally relevant to them.
new definition: To connect with people because your message feels relevant to them.
old example: The content that resonates most with our persona is not about features — it is about the feeling of finally being able to show the board that marketing is working.
new example: This message really resonates with our target audience.

old definition: To plan and visualise all the steps a customer takes from first awareness to purchase — and what they need at each stage.
new definition: To plan every step a customer takes before buying.
old example: We mapped out the customer journey and discovered that most prospects went cold between the second and third email — so we rewrote that sequence completely.
new example: Let's map out the customer journey before we write the emails.

old definition: To narrow down a large list of contacts by applying specific characteristics — so you can target the right people.
new definition: To reduce a long list by keeping only contacts that match certain features.
old example: Filter the database by company size, sector, and whether they have engaged with any content in the last 90 days — that gives you your warm segment.
new example: Please filter the database by company size and location.

old definition: To deeply understand how a customer thinks — their priorities, fears, and decision-making process.
new definition: To really understand how a person thinks and feels.
old example: Good persona work is about getting inside the customer's head — not just knowing their job title, but knowing what keeps them awake at three in the morning.
new example: She spent hours reading reports to get inside the customer's head.

old definition: Something your brand does well or has that competitors do not — an internal advantage you can build a marketing strategy around.
new definition: Something good that a company or brand does very well.
old example: TechFlow's biggest strength is its 98% client retention rate — that is exceptional in any market and we are going to make it the centrepiece of the campaign.
new example: Our biggest strength is our loyal customer base.

old definition: An internal limitation or gap that puts you at a disadvantage — something you need to either fix or work around in your marketing.
new definition: A problem inside a company that makes it less competitive.
old example: Our main weakness is brand awareness — we have excellent results but almost no one in our target market has heard of us yet.
new example: Our main weakness is that few people know our brand.

old definition: An external condition in the market that you can use to your advantage — a trend, a gap, or a competitor's weakness.
new definition: A chance in the market that a brand can use to grow.
old example: The biggest opportunity right now is that the market leader just increased their prices by 30% — several of their clients are actively looking for alternatives.
new example: The new social platform is a real opportunity for us.

old definition: An external factor that could hurt your brand's performance — a competitor move, a market shift, or a regulatory change.
new definition: Something outside a company that could cause it harm.
old example: The main threat is a well-funded new entrant who launched last quarter with aggressive pricing and a large marketing budget.
new example: A cheaper rival is the biggest threat to our sales.

old definition: To use an advantage, asset, or strength to get the best possible result — making the most of what you already have.
new definition: To use something you have to get the best result.
old example: We need to leverage those three client case studies — they are sitting in a folder on the server and no one is seeing them. They should be front and centre in every campaign.
new example: We should leverage our strong reviews in every ad.

old definition: To reduce the impact of a risk or weakness — to make it less of a problem through deliberate action.
new definition: To make a problem or risk smaller or less serious.
old example: We cannot eliminate the brand awareness weakness overnight, but we can mitigate it by getting three endorsements from recognisable industry figures in the first month.
new example: We can mitigate the risk by testing the ad first.

old definition: The full picture of who your competitors are, what they offer, and how they position themselves — the market environment your brand is operating in.
new definition: All the competitors in a market and how they compare.
old example: Before running the SWOT, spend an hour mapping the competitive landscape — who is in the market, what they are saying, and where the gaps are.
new example: The competitive landscape is crowded in our region.

old definition: A standard used to compare performance — either against a competitor, an industry average, or your own past results.
new definition: A standard that you use to compare results.
old example: The industry benchmark for email open rates in B2B SaaS is around 22%. Our last campaign hit 31% — that is a strength worth building on.
new example: The industry benchmark for open rates is around twenty percent.

old definition: To use an existing advantage as the foundation for your next move — rather than focusing only on what is not working.
new definition: To use something you do well as a base for growth.
old example: We built on the retention rate strength by making it the headline of every case study — '98% of clients renew. Here is why.'
new example: Let's build on our strength in video content.

old definition: To act quickly and decisively on a market opportunity before a competitor does.
new definition: To use a chance quickly and get a benefit from it.
old example: The market leader's price increase is our opportunity — we need to capitalise on it this quarter before they respond by adding value back in.
new example: We need to capitalise on this opportunity before our rivals do.

old definition: To take deliberate action to reduce or fix an internal limitation — not just acknowledge it.
new definition: To try to fix a problem inside your company.
old example: The SWOT identified three weaknesses — this quarter we are addressing the most urgent one: the lack of case studies in the manufacturing sector.
new example: This quarter we will address our weakness in email marketing.

old definition: To take proactive steps to reduce the impact of an external risk before it causes damage.
new definition: To protect yourself from an outside risk before it happens.
old example: The best way to guard against the new competitor's aggressive pricing is to stop competing on price and compete on results instead.
new example: We must guard against a threat from new low-cost competitors.

old definition: To reframe a limitation as something that can be used strategically — finding the upside in a gap.
new definition: To change a problem into something useful for the business.
old example: Being unknown in the market is a weakness — but we can turn it into an opportunity by positioning as the challenger brand that does things differently from the incumbents.
new example: Let's turn our small size into an opportunity to be more personal.

old definition: To finish a strategic review with a clear conclusion or actionable next step — not just observations.
new definition: To finish a review with clear results or decisions.
old example: A SWOT is only useful if you come out of it with three or four clear decisions. Otherwise it is just a list of things you already knew.
new example: We want to come out of the analysis with a clear plan.

old definition: Any channel where you pay to place your message in front of an audience — ads, sponsored posts, and paid search.
new definition: Advertising space or promotion that a company pays for to reach people.
old example: Paid media gives you speed — you can be in front of 50,000 targeted prospects tomorrow. The trade-off is that the moment you stop paying, the visibility stops too.
new example: We will use paid media to launch the new product.

old definition: Attention and coverage you get for free because someone else chose to share, mention, or feature you — PR, word of mouth, and organic shares.
new definition: Free attention from news, reviews, or people sharing your brand.
old example: Getting featured in an industry publication is earned media — you did not pay for it, which is why it carries more credibility than an ad.
new example: The magazine article was great earned media for our brand.

old definition: Channels you fully control — your website, email list, blog, and social media accounts.
new definition: Channels that a company controls, like its website and email list.
old example: Your email list is your most valuable owned media asset — you own it completely, no algorithm can take it away, and it converts better than almost any paid channel.
new example: Our newsletter is our strongest owned media channel.

old definition: A strategy where all channels work together to give the customer one consistent experience — regardless of where they first encounter the brand.
new definition: Using all channels together so customers have one smooth experience.
old example: An omnichannel campaign means someone who sees your LinkedIn ad, then reads your blog, then gets your email all feels like they are having one continuous conversation with your brand — not three separate ones.
new example: Our omnichannel plan connects social media, email, video, and events.

old definition: Working out which channel or touchpoint actually deserves credit for a conversion — which part of the journey made the sale happen.
new definition: Deciding which marketing step should get credit for a sale.
old example: Attribution is one of the hardest problems in marketing — a client might see a LinkedIn ad, read a blog post, open an email, and then book a call. Which one gets the credit?
new example: Attribution shows that search brought in most of our sales.

old definition: Content or traffic that reaches people without paid promotion — through search rankings, social algorithms, or genuine sharing.
new definition: Coming naturally from search or sharing, without paying for it.
old example: Organic reach takes longer to build than paid, but once it is working it brings consistent traffic without a media spend behind every piece of content.
new example: Organic growth on our blog has been slow but steady.

old definition: The number of people who see your content or campaign — how wide your message spreads.
new definition: The number of different people who see a message.
old example: The campaign had a reach of 180,000 people — but reach alone tells you nothing about quality. What matters is how many of those 180,000 matched the target persona.
new example: Her phone video gave the campaign a huge reach this week.

old definition: Any moment when a potential customer comes into contact with your brand — an ad, an email, a blog post, an event, or a sales call.
new definition: A point where a customer meets or interacts with a brand.
old example: Research shows B2B buyers need an average of 7 to 10 touchpoints before they are ready to have a serious conversation — which is why a single-channel strategy almost never works.
new example: Every touchpoint, from search to email, should feel consistent.

old definition: To make your message stand out in a crowded environment where the audience is bombarded with competing content.
new definition: To make a message stand out when there is too much content.
old example: The only way to cut through the noise on LinkedIn right now is specificity — a post written for one person always outperforms a post written for everyone.
new example: We need a bold headline to cut through the noise.

old definition: To increase your investment in a channel that is already working — rather than spreading budget equally across everything.
new definition: To spend more on a channel that is already working well.
old example: LinkedIn is generating 80% of our leads for a quarter of the budget. We should double down on it and pull back from the channels that are underperforming.
new example: Our paid ads perform best, so let's double down on them.

old definition: To use marketing activity to send people to a specific destination — a landing page, a case study, or a booking form.
new definition: To bring visitors to one specific web page.
old example: The LinkedIn campaign will drive traffic to the case study landing page — that is where the conversion happens, not in the ad itself.
new example: This campaign will drive traffic to our new pricing page.

old definition: To lose a potential customer at a specific point in the journey — when they stop engaging before completing the desired action.
new definition: To lose potential customers at one stage of the buying process.
old example: Our analytics show a significant drop-off between the landing page and the booking form — which tells us the page is not doing its job.
new example: We see a big drop off in the funnel at checkout.

old definition: To run a small, controlled campaign on a new channel to validate results before committing the full budget.
new definition: To try a channel on a small scale before spending more.
old example: Never scale a new channel before you test it — run a 30-day pilot with a limited budget, check the cost per lead, and then decide whether to invest more.
new example: Let's test video ads before scaling them across all markets.

old definition: To use the right content or channel at the right moment to take a prospect from one stage of the buying journey to the next.
new definition: To help a possible customer move to the next buying stage.
old example: The email sequence is designed to move prospects along the funnel — the first email builds awareness, the second shares proof, and the third invites a conversation.
new example: This email series will move leads along the funnel toward a purchase.

old definition: A core theme or topic that your brand owns and creates content around consistently — the foundation everything else is built on.
new definition: A main topic that a brand regularly creates content about.
old example: TechFlow's three content pillars are: operational efficiency, cost reduction, and manufacturing leadership. Every piece of content we produce connects to at least one of these.
new example: Our first content pillar is customer success stories.

old definition: The personality and style that comes through in all your written and spoken content — how your brand sounds, not just what it says.
new definition: The style and personality that shows in how a brand writes and speaks.
old example: TechFlow's tone of voice is direct, evidence-led, and peer-to-peer — we talk to operations directors like they are colleagues, not customers.
new example: Our tone of voice should be friendly but still professional.

old definition: A planned schedule of what content will be published, on which channel, and when — keeping the team organised and consistent.
new definition: A schedule showing what content will be published, where, and when.
old example: Without an editorial calendar, content becomes reactive — you publish when you have time, not when your audience needs it. With one, every week has a purpose.
new example: I added the new video to the editorial calendar for Thursday.

old definition: To take one piece of content and adapt it for a different format or channel — getting more value out of the same idea.
new definition: To change content so it can be used in a new format.
old example: We repurpose every case study into three formats: a long-form PDF, a LinkedIn carousel, and a short email. One story, three different ways to reach people who prefer different formats.
new example: Let's repurpose this report into a short email and a carousel.

old definition: Content that stays relevant and useful over a long period — not tied to a specific event or trend.
new definition: Content that stays useful and interesting for a long time.
old example: 'How to reduce operational costs by 20%' is evergreen content — someone will be searching for that in two years and the article will still be relevant. 'Our Q3 trade show recap' is not.
new example: This guide is evergreen, so we can share it all year.

old definition: Content that positions your brand or its people as trusted experts — sharing genuine insight rather than promoting products.
new definition: Content that shows a brand or person is a trusted expert.
old example: The best B2B thought leadership does not mention your product at all — it solves a problem your audience has, and the credibility from that is what brings them back.
new example: Her talk at the conference is great thought leadership for our company.

old definition: A review of all the content you have already created — assessing what is performing, what is outdated, and what gaps need to be filled.
new definition: A check of all existing content to see what works and what doesn't.
old example: Before creating new content, we always run a content audit. In TechFlow's case, they had twelve blog posts — three performing well, seven outdated, and two that needed a complete rewrite.
new example: We did a content audit and found many outdated blog posts.

old definition: The specific thing you want the reader or viewer to do next — download, book, read, share, or reply.
new definition: A message that tells the reader what action to take next.
old example: Every piece of content needs a clear call to action — even thought leadership. If someone reads your article and finds it useful, what do you want them to do next? That answer belongs at the end of every post.
new example: The call to action at the end of the email is too weak.

old definition: To launch and implement a content strategy in a structured, phased way.
new definition: To start using a plan in organised steps.
old example: We will roll out the content plan in three phases: foundation content in month one, case studies in month two, and thought leadership pieces in month three.
new example: We will roll out the content plan in three phases.

old definition: To create content that addresses a topic your audience needs but your competitors are not covering well.
new definition: To offer content on a topic that others are not covering well.
old example: There is almost no quality content on operational efficiency for mid-size manufacturers in English. We are going to fill that gap — and own the topic before anyone else does.
new example: Our new video series will fill a gap in the market.

old definition: To grow a following or readership over time through consistent, valuable content.
new definition: To slowly grow the number of people who follow or read your content.
old example: Building up a LinkedIn audience takes at least three to six months of consistent posting — there is no shortcut, but once the audience is there it compounds.
new example: We want to build up an audience on LinkedIn this year.

old definition: To make sure every piece of content is consistent with the brand's tone of voice, values, and positioning.
new definition: To keep content matching the brand's style, values, and image.
old example: Before anything goes live, ask: does this stay on brand? If TechFlow's tone is direct and evidence-led, a vague inspirational post does not belong in the plan.
new example: This post is funny, but it doesn't stay on brand.

old definition: To capture the reader's attention immediately — in the first line, headline, or opening image — so they keep reading.
new definition: To catch the reader's attention right away so they keep reading.
old example: The first line of any piece of content is the most important one. If it does not hook the reader in, they will not read the second line. Every post should open with something that makes your target audience think 'this is written for me'.
new example: A surprising statistic will hook the reader in from the first line.

old definition: To formally approve content before it is published — confirming it is accurate, on brand, and ready to go.
new definition: To give final approval for content before it is published.
old example: No content goes live without the client signing off on it — one approval loop avoids misunderstandings and protects both sides.
new example: The client still needs to sign off on the final article.

old definition: The percentage of people who opened your email out of everyone who received it — the first measure of whether your subject line worked.
new definition: The share of people who open an email they receive.
old example: The campaign achieved a 34% open rate, which is well above the B2B average of 22%.
new example: Our open rate went up after we changed the sender name.

old definition: The percentage of people who clicked a link inside your email — shows whether your content and call to action motivated people to take the next step.
new definition: The share of people who click a link in an email.
old example: A high open rate with a low click-through rate means the email was opened but the call to action did not work.
new example: The click-through rate was low, so we changed the button.

old definition: A method where you send two versions of the same email to different groups — changing one element — to find out which version performs better.
new definition: A test that sends two versions of an email to see which works better.
old example: The team ran an A/B test on the subject line and the second version had a 40% higher open rate.
new example: We ran an A/B test on two different subject lines.

old definition: A series of automated emails sent over time — each one designed to move the prospect one step closer to taking action.
new definition: A set of automatic emails sent one after another over time.
old example: The drip campaign sends five emails over three weeks to move prospects from awareness to a booked call.
new example: New subscribers get a welcome email from our drip campaign.

old definition: The percentage of people who opted out of your email list after receiving a campaign — a signal that the content is not relevant to them.
new definition: The share of people who stop getting your emails after a campaign.
old example: An unsubscribe rate above 0.5% is a warning sign that the content is not relevant to the audience.
new example: Our unsubscribe rate stayed low after last week's newsletter.

old definition: Whether your emails actually reach the recipient's inbox — rather than going to spam or being blocked by their email server.
new definition: How well your emails reach people's inboxes instead of spam folders.
old example: The open rate dropped because of a deliverability problem — the emails were going to spam instead of the inbox.
new example: Poor deliverability meant many of our emails went to spam.

old definition: Dividing your email list into groups based on shared characteristics — so you can send each group a more relevant, targeted message.
new definition: Splitting an email list into smaller groups with shared features.
old example: After applying segmentation to separate clients from prospects, the click-through rate on the prospect list doubled.
new example: Segmentation helps us send different offers to different customers.

old definition: The short text that appears in the inbox before an email is opened — the single most important factor in whether someone opens or ignores your email.
new definition: The short line of text people see before they open an email.
old example: A strong subject line either addresses a pain point, makes a specific promise, or creates genuine curiosity.
new example: We tested a shorter subject line to get more people to open it.

old definition: To remove invalid, inactive, or unengaged contacts from your email list — improving deliverability and engagement rates.
new definition: To remove old or wrong contacts from an email list.
old example: The team cleans the list every quarter by removing contacts who have not opened an email in six months.
new example: We clean the list every quarter to remove old email addresses.

old definition: To gradually re-engage a cold or inactive email list with lighter content before sending a conversion-focused campaign.
new definition: To slowly get an inactive email list interested again before a big send.
old example: A cold list was warmed up with three short emails before the main campaign was sent.
new example: We need to warm up the list before the big product launch.

old definition: Another term for A/B testing — to test two versions of an email element against each other to find the better performer.
new definition: To compare two versions of an email to see which does better.
old example: The team split tested the call to action button before launching the full campaign.
new example: We split test the headline before we send the campaign to everyone.

old definition: To send a second email to people who did not respond to the first — a common and effective tactic in B2B campaigns.
new definition: To send another email to people who did not answer the first one.
old example: The team always follows up on the first email because most conversions come from the second or third message.
new example: She will follow up on the email tomorrow morning.

old definition: To choose to receive (opt in) or stop receiving (opt out) emails from a brand — an essential part of email compliance and list management.
new definition: To agree to get emails from a brand, or to ask to stop.
old example: Every contact on the list has opted in through a content download or a direct signup form.
new example: Customers can opt in or opt out at any time.

old definition: To tailor the email content to the individual recipient — using their name, company, industry, or behaviour to make it feel written for them specifically.
new definition: To change an email so it fits each person who receives it.
old example: The team personalises each email by including the recipient's company name and the specific sector they work in.
new example: We personalise each email with the customer's first name.

old definition: An influencer with a smaller but highly engaged audience — typically 1,000 to 50,000 followers — who is trusted as an expert within a specific niche.
new definition: An influencer who has a small but loyal group of followers.
old example: In B2B, a micro-influencer with 8,000 followers in the manufacturing sector will outperform a generalist with 500,000. The audience is smaller but the trust is deeper and the fit is exact.
new example: She is a micro-influencer, so her followers trust her advice.

old definition: The total number of people who could potentially see a piece of content — the size of the audience an influencer has access to.
new definition: The number of people who can see a piece of content.
old example: Reach tells you the ceiling of how many people might see the content — but it says nothing about whether those people are the right audience or whether they actually trust the influencer.
new example: This influencer has a huge reach, but her audience is quite general.

old definition: The quality of being genuine — an influencer who truly uses and believes in what they recommend, rather than just taking a fee to promote it.
new definition: The quality of being real and honest, not fake.
old example: Audiences can detect inauthenticity immediately — if an influencer recommends your product but has no real experience of it, the post will not convert and may actually damage the brand.
new example: Her authenticity is why her followers believe every product she recommends.

old definition: A public statement of support or recommendation from an influencer or authority figure — they are putting their name behind your brand.
new definition: A public statement that supports or recommends a product or brand.
old example: A genuine endorsement from a respected industry analyst is worth more than a paid post from a large influencer — because the audience trusts the analyst's judgement, not just their reach.
new example: He gave our new headphones a strong endorsement in his latest video.

old definition: User-Generated Content — content created by real users or customers about your brand, rather than by your marketing team. Highly trusted because it is not paid for.
new definition: Content about a brand that customers make themselves, not the brand.
old example: When clients post their own results from using TechFlow and tag us, that is UGC — and it converts better than any ad we create ourselves because it is completely unprompted.
new example: She loved the UGC from customers, so we shared it on our page.

old definition: The percentage of an influencer's audience who actively interact with their content — likes, comments, shares, and replies.
new definition: The share of followers who like, comment on or share posts.
old example: An influencer with 50,000 followers and a 0.5% engagement rate is less valuable than one with 8,000 followers and a 6% engagement rate. The second audience is actively listening.
new example: Her engagement rate is much higher than the other influencer's.

old definition: A collaboration between your brand and an influencer — where both sides get something of value from working together.
new definition: A working relationship where both sides gain something useful.
old example: The best influencer partnerships feel like genuine collaborations, not transactions — the influencer is involved in the process, their voice comes through, and the audience can tell it is real.
new example: We are happy about our new partnership with a popular creator.

old definition: A very specific, focused area of interest or expertise — the topic an influencer is known for and trusted on.
new definition: A small, specific area of interest that a group of people follow.
old example: The influencer's niche is operational efficiency in manufacturing — 9,000 followers, but every single one is in our exact target market. That is more valuable than 200,000 general business followers.
new example: Her niche is skincare for sensitive skin, so she suits our brand.

old definition: To make the first contact with an influencer — introducing your brand and proposing a potential partnership.
new definition: To contact an influencer for the first time.
old example: Before you reach out, spend two weeks engaging with their content genuinely — comment thoughtfully, share their posts, respond to their questions. Cold outreach from a brand they have never heard of is almost always ignored.
new example: I will reach out to her today about our new campaign.

old definition: To share the same beliefs, principles, and standards as the brand — essential before any influencer partnership can work.
new definition: To share the same beliefs and standards as a brand.
old example: Check whether the influencer aligns with your brand values before you approach them. An influencer who takes every sponsorship regardless of fit will not be credible when they recommend you.
new example: We need an influencer who aligns with our brand's values.

old definition: To propose a collaboration to an influencer — explaining what you are offering, what you are asking for, and why it is a good fit for both sides.
new definition: To suggest a working plan to an influencer and explain why it is good.
old example: When you pitch a partnership, lead with what is in it for them — not what you want. 'Here is why this would be interesting content for your audience' lands better than 'here is our product and what we would like you to say about it'.
new example: I will pitch a partnership to her this afternoon.

old definition: To publicly state that content is sponsored or paid for — a legal requirement in most markets and an ethical standard in influencer marketing.
new definition: To tell people clearly that a post was paid for.
old example: Always disclose the partnership — not just because it is required by law, but because audiences respect transparency and it actually increases trust rather than reducing it.
new example: You must disclose a partnership in every sponsored post.

old definition: To establish trust and authority through consistent, genuine, high-quality content or associations.
new definition: To make people trust and respect you over time.
old example: A long-term partnership with two or three trusted voices in your industry builds credibility much faster than ten short-term sponsored posts with whoever is available.
new example: Working with experts will help us build credibility with new customers.

old definition: To produce content together with an influencer — combining their knowledge and audience access with your brand's story.
new definition: To make content together with another person or brand.
old example: Co-creating a case study with the influencer — they write it in their own voice from their perspective — is far more powerful than briefing them to promote a PDF you already produced.
new example: We want to co-create content with him for the next campaign.

old definition: The story that runs through all your marketing — the way you explain who you are, what you do, and why it matters, in a connected and meaningful way.
new definition: The connected story that explains who a brand is and why it matters.
old example: TechFlow's narrative should not be 'we make software for manufacturers' — it should be 'we give operations directors the evidence they need to walk into the board meeting with confidence'.
new example: Our narrative needs to focus on the customer, not the product.

old definition: The central character in a marketing story — in B2B, the hero is almost always the client, not the brand.
new definition: The main character of a story, who faces a problem and succeeds.
old example: The biggest mistake in brand storytelling is making the brand the hero. Your client is the hero — they faced a challenge, they made a decision, and they achieved a result. Your brand is the tool that helped them get there.
new example: In our case study, the client is the hero.

old definition: The problem or challenge that creates tension in the story — the obstacle the hero has to overcome.
new definition: The problem or struggle that makes a story tense and interesting.
old example: The conflict in TechFlow's best case study is simple: the client was told to cut operational costs by 20% or face redundancies — and they had 90 days to do it.
new example: The conflict in this story is a tight budget and a short deadline.

old definition: The point in the story where the problem is solved and the outcome becomes clear — how the hero successfully overcame the conflict.
new definition: The part of a story where the problem is solved.
old example: The resolution: in 67 days — 23 days ahead of schedule — the client hit 22% cost reduction with no redundancies and a 98% team satisfaction score. That is a resolution worth reading.
new example: The resolution shows the client finishing early and saving money.

old definition: Content that connects with how people feel — not just what they think — making a message more memorable and motivating.
new definition: A way of connecting with an audience through their feelings.
old example: The emotional appeal in that case study is not the 22% number — it is the relief of not having to make redundancies. That is what makes the operations director reading it think: 'I need this'.
new example: The video uses emotional appeal to make people feel proud of their families.

old definition: The change that the hero goes through — from where they were before to where they are after. The before-and-after is the heart of any case study.
new definition: A big change from how things were before to how they are after.
old example: The transformation is: from a director under impossible pressure with no clear path, to someone who delivered results ahead of schedule and got promoted six months later. That arc is the story.
new example: The case study shows the transformation of a small shop into a growing brand.

old definition: A specific, verifiable piece of evidence that supports your story — a number, a quote, a result, or a data point.
new definition: A fact, number or quote that shows a claim is true.
old example: Every story needs proof points — without them it is just a claim. '22% cost reduction in 67 days' is a proof point. 'Significant operational improvements' is not.
new example: This customer survey is a strong proof point for our campaign.

old definition: The overarching narrative that explains why your brand exists, what it stands for, and what it has achieved — told in a way that connects with people emotionally as well as logically.
new definition: The story of why a company exists and what it believes.
old example: TechFlow's brand story is not about software. It is about operations directors who refuse to accept the false choice between cutting costs and keeping their team — and how TechFlow makes that possible.
new example: Our brand story starts with a small family workshop.

old definition: To tell a story in a way that feels vivid and real — using specific details, quotes, and human moments rather than abstract claims.
new definition: To make a story feel vivid, real and interesting.
old example: Numbers alone do not bring a story to life — the moment that does is when the client says: 'The week before we hit the target, I genuinely did not think we were going to make it.' That one sentence makes the 22% feel real.
new example: Let's add customer quotes to bring the story to life.

old definition: To start a story by describing the challenge or conflict before introducing the solution — because the audience needs to recognise the problem before they care about the answer.
new definition: To begin a story with the problem before the solution.
old example: Always lead with the problem in a case study — not your product. If the reader does not immediately think 'that is exactly my situation', they will not read far enough to care about the solution.
new example: In the presentation, we should lead with the problem our customers face.

old definition: To position the client or customer as the central character who overcame a challenge — with your brand as the tool or guide that helped them.
new definition: To show the customer as the main character who succeeds.
old example: Rewrite that case study to make the operations director the hero — her courage, her decision, her result. TechFlow is the platform that made it possible. The moment you make TechFlow the hero, you lose the reader.
new example: In this campaign, we want to make her the hero.

old definition: To capture the audience's attention and make them want to keep reading or listening — usually by creating a sense of tension or relevance.
new definition: To get people's attention and make them want to know more.
old example: The opening line of the case study needs to draw the reader in immediately — something like 'In October 2025, Claire had 90 days to save 40 jobs. She did not know it yet, but she was going to do it in 67.' That is how you make someone read to the end.
new example: A short, surprising headline will draw readers in.

old definition: For a story or message to connect and stick with the audience — to be understood and remembered in the way you intended.
new definition: For a message to be understood and remembered by people.
old example: The story needs one more draft — the resolution does not land yet. The reader gets to the end without feeling the significance of what happened. Add the human moment and the number will land much harder.
new example: The message did not land with younger customers in our survey.

old definition: To support what you are saying with specific, verifiable proof — so the audience trusts the story rather than just enjoying it.
new definition: To support an idea with facts, numbers or other proof.
old example: Every claim in a case study needs to be backed up with a proof point. 'Significantly improved efficiency' means nothing. '22% cost reduction measured over 90 days against the previous financial year' means everything.
new example: We need to back up this claim with evidence from real customers.

old definition: A visual summary of your most important marketing metrics in one place — giving you a quick overview of performance across channels.
new definition: A screen that shows key numbers and results in one place.
old example: Every Monday morning I check the dashboard first — it tells me in two minutes whether we are on track or whether something needs attention before I read the detail.
new example: I check the dashboard every morning before the team meeting.

old definition: A specific, meaningful conclusion drawn from data — not just a number, but what the number means and what you should do about it.
new definition: A useful conclusion that you learn from studying data.
old example: The data shows a 40% drop in LinkedIn engagement on Fridays. The insight is not 'engagement drops on Fridays' — the insight is 'do not publish thought leadership on Fridays; our audience is not in work mode'.
new example: She shared a great insight about our email audience.

old definition: A specific subset of your audience or data — grouped by shared characteristics to allow more targeted analysis and action.
new definition: A smaller group of people taken from a larger audience.
old example: When we split the conversion data by segment — manufacturing versus logistics — the difference was dramatic. Manufacturing converts at 4.2x the rate of logistics. That changes our entire channel allocation.
new example: This segment of customers opens our emails more than any other.

old definition: A group of users or contacts who share a common starting point — for example, everyone who signed up in Q1 or everyone who downloaded the case study in October.
new definition: A group of people who start or do something at the same time.
old example: We track cohorts to understand retention: the October cohort — everyone who booked a discovery call after the webinar — had a 68% conversion to proposal rate. That is three times our historical average.
new example: The October cohort stayed with us longer than the others.

old definition: A single piece of information in a dataset — meaningful only when seen in context alongside other data points.
new definition: One single piece of information in a set of data.
old example: A single data point — like one month's low open rate — means very little on its own. Three consecutive months of declining open rate is a trend that requires action.
new example: This one data point stands out from all the others.

old definition: A consistent direction or pattern in data over time — either improving or declining — that tells you something is changing.
new definition: A general direction in which numbers change over a period of time.
old example: The trend in LinkedIn organic reach is consistently up — 12% month on month for four months. That tells us the content strategy is working and we should invest more, not change course.
new example: The trend in our website visits has been going up all year.

old definition: A reference standard used to evaluate performance — either an industry average, a competitor comparison, or your own historical best.
new definition: A standard that you compare your results with.
old example: Always present results against a benchmark — '3.8% click-through rate' is meaningless without context. '3.8% click-through rate, versus an industry benchmark of 2.5%' tells the client they are performing above average.
new example: Our click rate is above the industry benchmark this quarter.

old definition: The percentage of people who took a specific desired action — clicked, downloaded, booked, or bought — out of everyone who had the opportunity to do so.
new definition: The share of visitors who complete a wanted action, shown as a percentage.
old example: Our landing page conversion rate is 11% — for every 100 people who visit the page, 11 book a call. That is strong. The question now is: are the right 100 people getting to the page?
new example: Our conversion rate went up after we changed the landing page.

old definition: To retrieve and compile data from a platform or tool for review or presentation.
new definition: To collect information from a system so you can look at it.
old example: Before the client meeting, pull the data from LinkedIn, HubSpot, and the email platform — I want everything in one view so we can see the full picture.
new example: Can you pull the data from our email tool before the meeting?

old definition: To go beyond the top-level data and look at the specific detail underneath — to find out what is driving the headline number.
new definition: To look closely at the small details behind the main results.
old example: The overall conversion rate looks good — but when we drill down into the data by channel, we find that LinkedIn is converting at 12% and email is converting at 1.3%. That is where the real insight is.
new example: Let's drill down into the numbers to see why sales dropped.

old definition: To identify and bring attention to a problem or anomaly in the data — before it becomes a bigger issue.
new definition: To point out a problem so that other people notice it.
old example: I want to flag something in the data before we move on: the cost per lead on paid search jumped 180% this month. That is not a seasonal change — something specific happened and we need to find out what.
new example: I need to flag an issue with last week's ad results.

old definition: To monitor a metric consistently across multiple periods — to identify trends rather than reacting to individual data points.
new definition: To watch how results change across weeks, months or years.
old example: Track conversion rate over time, not just month to month — a single bad month means little, but four months of gradual decline tells you something structural has changed.
new example: She likes to track performance over time on her screen every week.

old definition: To make a specific decision or change based on what the data revealed — the whole point of data analysis.
new definition: To do something useful because of what you have learned.
old example: The insight is clear — manufacturing clients convert at 4x the rate of logistics clients. The action is clear too: shift 70% of the campaign budget to manufacturing audiences from next month.
new example: We need to take action on this insight before the campaign ends.

old definition: To establish the starting point against which future performance will be measured.
new definition: To decide on the first measurement that you will compare later results with.
old example: Month one is about setting a baseline — we are not expecting record results, we are establishing what normal looks like for TechFlow so we can measure improvement accurately from month two.
new example: In the first month, we will set a baseline for our website traffic.

old definition: A planned list of topics to be discussed in a meeting — shared in advance so everyone arrives prepared.
new definition: A list of topics to be discussed at a meeting.
old example: The team sends the agenda 24 hours before every meeting so everyone can prepare.
new example: I'll go through the agenda with the client before our call.

old definition: A specific task that needs to be completed after the meeting — with a clear owner and a deadline.
new definition: A task that someone must do after a meeting.
old example: Every meeting ends with clear action items — each one has a specific owner and a deadline.
new example: Her first action item is to update the campaign budget.

old definition: A written record of what was discussed and decided in a meeting — including action items, owners, and deadlines.
new definition: A written record of what was said and decided in a meeting.
old example: The team sends the minutes within 24 hours of every meeting to confirm what was agreed.
new example: Could you send the minutes to the whole marketing team?

old definition: To give a brief, clear overview of what has been discussed or decided — capturing the key points without repeating everything.
new definition: To give a short overview of the main points.
old example: At the end of each agenda item, the chair summarises what was agreed before moving on.
new example: Let me summarise the main results of this month's campaign.

old definition: Communication or action that happens after a meeting to check progress on what was agreed or to provide additional information.
new definition: A message or action after a meeting to check progress.
old example: A follow-up email is sent after every client meeting with action items, owners, and deadlines.
new example: She is writing a follow-up email to the client after the call.
