old definition: Use this phrase to introduce what a reputation management document addresses — which situations it covers, who is responsible, what the response timelines are, and how decisions get made under pressure. It belongs in leadership presentations and team briefings when launching a new plan.
new definition: A way to explain what a reputation plan includes.
old example: Dana presented the plan: The reputation management plan covers four scenarios — a viral negative post, a media inquiry on a sensitive topic, a product or service failure, and a data or security incident. For each scenario, the plan defines who is the lead spokesperson, what the response timeline is, who approves the statement before it goes out, and which channels we respond on. Nobody should need to improvise in a crisis.
new example: The reputation management plan covers product recalls and bad reviews.

old definition: Demand-Side Platform — the technology advertisers and agencies use to buy digital ad space automatically. A DSP connects to multiple ad exchanges and SSPs, so buyers can set their targeting, bidding rules, and budgets all in one place. The 'demand side' means the buyer's side of the deal.
new definition: Short for demand-side platform: a tool advertisers use to buy ads automatically.
old example: Riley explained the tech stack to the client: We use a DSP to manage all your programmatic buys. Instead of going to each publisher individually, the DSP lets us access inventory across thousands of websites and apps simultaneously. We set your targeting parameters, your bid limits, and your daily budget — and the platform optimises the buying automatically throughout the day.
new example: We use a DSP to buy ads on hundreds of websites.

old definition: Supply-Side Platform — the technology publishers use to sell their ad space to multiple buyers at the same time through ad exchanges and DSPs. An SSP helps a publisher get the most revenue possible from their available ad space by opening it up to many buyers at once. The 'supply side' means the publisher's side of the deal.
new definition: Short for supply-side platform: a tool websites use to sell ad space.
old example: Dana explained both sides of the ecosystem: When a user loads the Financial Times homepage, the FT's SSP sends a signal to multiple ad exchanges simultaneously saying: 'I have an impression available from a 45-year-old finance professional in London. What will you bid?' Our DSP receives that signal and decides within milliseconds whether to bid and how much. The SSP and DSP are the two sides of the same transaction.
new example: The news site sells its ad space through an SSP.

old definition: Real-Time Bidding — the automated auction through which programmatic ad space is bought and sold. When a user loads a web page, an RTB auction happens in milliseconds: multiple DSPs bid for the impression, the highest bid wins, and the ad appears before the page finishes loading. RTB lets advertisers bid on individual impressions, not just fixed placements.
new definition: Short for real-time bidding: an instant online auction for ad space.
old example: Marcus explained the speed to the client: The whole RTB process happens in under 100 milliseconds — faster than a human blink. While the page is loading, the SSP calls an auction, DSPs receive the bid request, evaluate whether the impression matches their targeting criteria, calculate a bid price, submit it, and the winner's ad is served. All of that happens before you've even seen the page.
new example: With RTB, the ad space is sold in less than a second.

old definition: A small file stored on a user's browser that tracks what they do across websites — pages visited, products viewed, actions taken. Cookies are the backbone of programmatic targeting, letting advertisers reach people based on their online behaviour. Third-party cookies — set by advertisers, not the website itself — are being phased out by major browsers, which is changing how programmatic targeting works.
new definition: A small file that records what someone does online.
old example: Riley addressed the client's question: Cookies are how we know you're bidding for someone who visited your pricing page three times last week but hasn't converted. The retargeting campaign reads the cookie that was placed when they visited your site and makes sure your ad follows them across the web. The challenge is that third-party cookies are being deprecated — we need to start planning alternative targeting approaches now.
new example: The cookie shows that this user visited our shoe page.

old definition: A specific rule used to decide which users should see an ad. Targeting parameters include demographics (age, gender, location), behaviours (recent website visits, purchase history), context (the content on the page where the ad appears), and audience segments (job title, industry, interest category). The more precise the targeting, the more relevant each impression — but the smaller your available audience.
new definition: A rule that decides who sees an ad.
old example: Dana set the targeting parameters for the campaign: For this campaign, I'm using three stacked targeting parameters — job title contains 'Head of Marketing' or 'CMO', company size between 50 and 500 employees, and industry: financial services or legal. That narrows the audience significantly but makes each impression much more valuable. We'd rather reach 8,000 perfect-fit prospects than 800,000 generic ones.
new example: Our main targeting parameter is age: 25 to 40.

old definition: The percentage of ads that are actually seen by a real person — not hidden below the fold, not covered by another element, not shown to a bot. The industry standard for a 'viewable' display ad is that at least 50% of the ad's pixels must be visible for at least one second. Low viewability means you are paying for ads nobody sees.
new definition: How often an ad is really seen by a person.
old example: Marcus reviewed the campaign report: Our viewability rate last month was 41%. The industry benchmark is 70%. That means 59% of our impressions were not technically seen. Either the ad placement is too far down the page, or we're buying from low-quality inventory. We need to set a viewability floor of 70% as a targeting parameter to filter out placements that don't meet that standard.
new example: Our viewability is 70%, so most people see the ad.

old definition: A limit on how many times a single user sees the same ad within a set time period. Frequency capping stops ad fatigue — when someone sees the same ad too many times, they start ignoring it or even resenting the brand. Common caps are 3–5 impressions per user per week.
new definition: A limit on how many times one person sees the same ad.
old example: Riley flagged the issue: Our frequency cap is currently set at 20 impressions per user per week — that's far too high. Some users in the retargeting pool are seeing this ad multiple times a day. Ad fatigue sets in after 5 or 6 exposures and after that point you're wasting spend and potentially damaging brand perception. Drop the frequency cap to 4 per week and watch what happens to CTR.
new example: We set a frequency cap of three ads per day.

old definition: Steps taken to make sure ads do not appear next to content that could hurt the brand's reputation — such as fake news, extreme content, violence, or adult material. Brand safety settings in a DSP use keyword blocklists and category exclusions to keep ads out of harmful environments.
new definition: Keeping ads away from content that could harm the brand.
old example: Dana briefed the client on the controls: Brand safety is built into our DSP setup for every campaign. We use a category exclusion list that blocks placement next to content flagged as misinformation, adult, violence, or politically inflammatory. We also use a keyword blocklist — if the page contains any of these 200 keywords, the bid is automatically suppressed. Your ad will not appear next to something that damages your reputation.
new example: For brand safety, our ads never appear next to violent news.

word: THE DSP OPTIMISES THE BUYING AUTOMATICALLY
old definition: Use this phrase to explain how the platform handles bidding, targeting, and budget without you having to manage it every minute. 'Optimises automatically' means the system uses data to adjust bids in real time to get the best performance within the limits you set. It's useful when explaining programmatic to clients who are new to ad tech.
new definition: A way to say the platform improves ad buying by itself.
old example: Marcus explained the value to the client: Once we set the targeting parameters, bid ceiling, and daily budget, the DSP optimises the buying automatically — it will bid more for impressions that match the highest-value audience characteristics and less for lower-value ones. You don't need to monitor it manually; the algorithm is doing that continuously. We review performance weekly and make strategic adjustments, but the day-to-day buying decisions are handled by the platform.
new example: The DSP optimises the buying automatically, so we save time.

word: WE SET A FLOOR PRICE TO FILTER OUT LOW-QUALITY INVENTORY
old definition: Use this phrase to describe using minimum bid prices or viewability floors to cut out low-quality ad placements. A 'floor price' is the lowest CPM (cost per thousand impressions) the DSP will accept — anything cheaper is usually low-quality inventory or bot traffic. Common in campaign setup and quality discussions.
new definition: A way to say a minimum price keeps out poor ad spaces.
old example: Riley explained the quality strategy: We've set a floor price of £3 CPM to filter out low-quality inventory. Anything below that price point is typically remnant inventory with low viewability, high bot traffic, or poor-quality placement. It costs us more per impression, but the quality of the impressions we buy is dramatically higher — and that translates to better CTR and lower cost-per-conversion.
new example: We set a floor price to filter out low-quality inventory on cheap sites.

word: THE CAMPAIGN IS TARGETING BASED ON...
old definition: Use this phrase to describe how the audience for a programmatic campaign is defined. It belongs in briefings with clients, internal teams, or platform partners — explaining who will see the ads and why. Always follow it with specific targeting criteria, not vague descriptions like 'marketing professionals'.
new definition: A way to explain how you choose the audience.
old example: Dana briefed the client on the setup: The campaign is targeting based on three stacked parameters: job title, company size, and recent website behaviour. Layer one — anyone who has visited the pricing page in the last 30 days. Layer two — within that pool, only those whose LinkedIn profile indicates they're a marketing decision-maker. Layer three — company size between 100 and 1,000 employees. That's a precision audience of about 12,000 people.
new example: The campaign is targeting based on interests and location.

word: THE THIRD-PARTY COOKIE IS BEING PHASED OUT
old definition: A phrase for the industry-wide change that is removing the main targeting tool in programmatic advertising. Major browsers — Chrome, Safari, Firefox — are removing third-party cookie support, which means the whole industry has to find new ways to identify and target users. Use it in planning conversations about what comes next.
new definition: A way to say an old tracking tool is slowly disappearing.
old example: Riley explained the strategic risk: The third-party cookie is being phased out — Google's Chrome is the last major browser to maintain it, and it's going away within the next 12 months. That means the retargeting model we rely on — identifying past website visitors across the web — will no longer work in the same way. We need a first-party data strategy now, not after the cookie disappears.
new example: The third-party cookie is being phased out, so we need new data.

word: WE NEED TO SET A FREQUENCY CAP TO AVOID AD FATIGUE
old definition: Use this phrase when recommending that a campaign limit how many times the same user sees the same ad. 'Ad fatigue' is what happens when someone sees an ad too often — they stop responding to it or start to dislike the brand. A frequency cap puts a limit on how many times the same person can see the ad in a given time period.
new definition: A way to say limit repeats so people don't get bored.
old example: Dana flagged the creative fatigue risk: We need to set a frequency cap to avoid ad fatigue — the current setup has no cap, which means some users in the retargeting pool are being shown this ad 15 to 20 times a week. After about five exposures, CTR typically drops by 60% and negative sentiment starts to build. I'm setting the cap at five per week and rotating the creative every two weeks.
new example: We need to set a frequency cap to avoid ad fatigue.

old definition: Use this phrase to describe what content or categories you have blocked from your campaign — the inventory you will not bid on. It belongs in campaign setup briefings, reporting, and quality assurance conversations. Always follow it with the specific list of excluded categories or the reason behind the keyword blocklist.
new definition: A way to say which content your ads will avoid.
old example: Marcus confirmed the brand safety setup to the client: The brand safety settings exclude six content categories: adult content, political advertising, misinformation and disinformation, violence and graphic content, gambling, and competing financial services brands. We've also built a 250-keyword blocklist that suppresses bids on any page containing terms associated with those categories. Your ads will only appear in professionally appropriate, brand-safe environments.
new example: The brand safety settings exclude gambling and adult websites.

old definition: The identity of a company — including its name, logo, values, and the way it presents itself to the world.
new definition: The name, logo and style of a company.
old example: Our brand stands for clarity, trust, and results — every piece of content we create should reflect those three things.
new example: Our brand uses black and gold in every shop.

old definition: A short description of a company, person, or product that gives the key facts and information.
new definition: A short text with the main facts about a company.
old example: Dana wrote a one-page brand profile that included the company's mission, values, target market, and main services.
new example: He is writing our company profile on his laptop.

old definition: The combination of things that make a brand unique — its look, values, voice, and the way it communicates.
new definition: What makes a brand different and easy to know.
old example: The agency's brand identity is modern and professional — clean design, clear language, and a consistent blue and white colour palette.
new example: Blue and white are part of our brand identity.

old definition: A principle or belief that is important to a company and guides how it behaves and makes decisions.
new definition: An important belief that guides a company.
old example: Our core values are honesty, quality, and partnership — they guide every decision we make as a team.
new example: Honesty is our most important value.

old definition: The main idea or feeling that a brand wants to communicate to its audience.
new definition: The main idea a brand wants to tell people.
old example: Our core message is simple: we help B2B companies grow without wasting time or money on marketing that does not work.
new example: Our message is simple: we save you time.

old definition: The specific group of people a brand wants to reach and communicate with.
new definition: The people a brand wants to talk to.
old example: Our audience is marketing managers at mid-sized B2B technology companies — they are busy, data-driven, and results-focused.
new example: Our audience is busy office workers.

old definition: The way a brand communicates — its personality and style. For example: formal, friendly, bold, or calm.
new definition: The way a brand speaks, like formal or friendly.
old example: Our tone is confident and clear — we are professional but we do not use unnecessary jargon.
new example: Our tone is friendly, not formal.

old definition: The same every time — not changing in quality, style, or approach. A consistent brand looks and sounds the same across all channels.
new definition: The same every time.
old example: Strong brands are consistent — the tone, design, and message are the same on LinkedIn, on the website, and in emails.
new example: Our logo is consistent on every product.

old definition: To represent or embody a set of values or principles — what a brand believes in.
new definition: To show what you believe in.
old example: Our brand stands for clarity and trust — every interaction we have with clients should reflect those values.
new example: We stand for trust and quality.

old definition: To be noticeably different from competitors — to be more visible, interesting, or memorable.
new definition: To be different and easy to notice.
old example: We stand out from the competition because we specialize in B2B — we are not a general marketing agency.
new example: Bright colours help us stand out from the competition.

old definition: To give a particular impression — the way your brand appears to other people.
new definition: To give people a certain feeling about you.
old example: We want to come across as professional and approachable — not cold or corporate.
new example: We want to come across as friendly and professional.

old definition: To develop and grow a brand over time — making it more well-known and trusted.
new definition: To make a brand known and trusted over time.
old example: Building a brand takes time — consistency is the most important thing you can do.
new example: It takes years to build a brand.

old definition: To communicate or explain something clearly — to make sure your message is understood.
new definition: To say an idea clearly so people understand.
old example: Our LinkedIn posts put across our key message: we deliver results, not just activity.
new example: She can put across our message in one minute.

old definition: To make something feel real and interesting — to express an idea in a way that people can connect with.
new definition: To make an idea feel real and exciting.
old example: Case studies are a great way to bring your brand values to life — they show what you do in a real context.
new example: His drawings bring our brand to life.

old definition: A group of products or services packaged and sold together — usually at a lower combined price than buying each separately.
new definition: A group of products sold together for a lower price.
old example: Riley offered the client a bundle that included content creation, LinkedIn management, and monthly reporting — all for one fixed price.
new example: This bundle costs $49 instead of $77.

old definition: The quality of staying with one company or supplier over time — often rewarded with special discounts or benefits.
new definition: Staying with the same company for a long time.
old example: We have a loyalty discount for clients who renew for a second year — they get fifteen percent off their renewal price.
new example: We give a loyalty card to our regular customers.

old definition: A special offer or deal — usually available for a limited time — designed to encourage people to buy.
new definition: A special offer for a short time.
old example: Our spring promotion includes a free strategy session for any client who signs up before the end of April.
new example: Our spring promotion ends next Friday.

old definition: A document or code that gives the holder a specific discount or benefit when they buy a product or service.
new definition: A ticket or code that gives you money off.
old example: Dana sent a voucher code to twenty warm leads — it gave them ten percent off their first month with no minimum commitment.
new example: This voucher gives you 10% off.

old definition: Something that motivates someone to take action — a reward or benefit that makes an offer more attractive.
new definition: Something that makes people want to do something.
old example: The main incentive for signing up this month is the free audit — we review your current LinkedIn presence and give you a detailed report at no cost.
new example: A free gift is a good incentive to sign up.

old definition: An agreement to do something or to continue with something for a period of time — often used in contracts.
new definition: A promise to stay with something for a set time.
old example: Our starter plan has no long-term commitment — clients can cancel after the first month if they are not satisfied.
new example: Our basic plan has no long commitment.

old definition: When a client continues with a service after the initial contract period ends — they choose to sign again.
new definition: When a customer continues a service for another period.
old example: Our renewal rate is very high — eighty percent of clients choose to continue after their first six-month contract.
new example: Your contract renewal is in January.

old definition: Available only to a specific group of people or for a limited time — not offered to everyone.
new definition: Only for a special group of people.
old example: This is an exclusive offer for clients who attended our webinar — it is not available on our website.
new example: This is an exclusive offer for our VIP customers.

old definition: To include something extra for free as part of an offer — to add a bonus without increasing the price.
new definition: To add something extra for free.
old example: If you sign up for the six-month plan, we will throw in a free brand audit at the start — that is worth €500 on its own.
new example: We'll throw in a free gift with every order.

old definition: To accept and use an offer that has been made to you.
new definition: To accept an offer.
old example: Out of the twenty clients who received the promotion email, eight took up the offer within the first week.
new example: He decided to take up an offer on his tablet.

old definition: To agree on a price now so that it is fixed and will not change — even if prices increase later.
new definition: To fix a price so it doesn't change.
old example: If you sign up before the end of the month, you lock in the current price for the full year — it will not go up at renewal.
new example: Sign up today to lock in the price of $149.

old definition: To make an offer more attractive by adding something extra.
new definition: To make an offer better by adding something.
old example: The client was on the fence, so Riley offered to sweeten the deal by including a monthly strategy call at no extra cost.
new example: To sweeten the deal, she offered one free month.

old definition: To formally agree to take a service or plan — to register or commit.
new definition: To join or register for a service.
old example: We are running a promotion this month — clients who sign up for a six-month plan get the first month free.
new example: You can sign up for our plan online.

old definition: To include something as part of a package or offer.
new definition: To include something.
old example: Every plan comes with a dedicated account manager and a monthly performance report — there are no hidden extras.
new example: All our plans come with a monthly report.

old definition: A short piece of content that hints at something coming — used to build curiosity and excitement before a launch.
new definition: A short post or video that gives a small hint about something new.
old example: We posted three teaser videos on LinkedIn in the week before the launch — each one revealed a small detail about the new service.
new example: Our first teaser just says 'Coming soon'.

old definition: The moment when a new product, service, or campaign is shown to the public for the first time — often a planned event or announcement.
new definition: The moment you show something new for the first time.
old example: The reveal happened live on a LinkedIn event — over 300 people watched as Riley unveiled the new platform name and features.
new example: She did the reveal on stage in front of 300 people.

old definition: A series of posts or communications leading up to a launch date — building anticipation day by day.
new definition: Counting the time until an event starts.
old example: We ran a five-day countdown on LinkedIn — each day a new post gave the audience one more reason to attend the launch event.
new example: We started a five-day countdown on social media.

old definition: The feeling of excitement and interest while waiting for something to happen — what a good teaser campaign creates.
new definition: Excitement while you wait for something.
old example: The teaser campaign built a lot of anticipation — by launch day, over 200 people had already registered for the event.
new example: The crowd was full of anticipation before the launch.

old definition: A plan that shows when each task or activity will happen — from now until the launch date.
new definition: A plan that shows when each step happens.
old example: Dana built a detailed timeline for the launch — week one was teaser content, week two was the event, week three was follow-up.
new example: Our timeline has three steps: teaser, event and rollout.

old definition: An important stage or event in a project — a key point that marks progress towards the final goal.
new definition: An important point in a project.
old example: We set three milestones for the launch: teaser campaign live, event registration open, and reveal day.
new example: Opening event registration is our first milestone.

old definition: A planned event — online or in person — where a new product or service is officially introduced to an audience.
new definition: An event where a new product is shown to people.
old example: The launch event was a 45-minute LinkedIn Live session — Riley presented the new service and answered questions from the audience.
new example: Over 300 people came to our launch event.

old definition: The process of making a new product or service available — often done gradually, starting with a small group.
new definition: Making something new available to people step by step.
old example: After the launch event, the rollout began — existing clients got access first, then new sign-ups from the following week.
new example: The rollout starts with our current customers.

old definition: To create growing excitement or anticipation in the period leading up to an event or launch.
new definition: To slowly create excitement before something happens.
old example: We are going to build up to the reveal with a week of teaser content — each post will give the audience one more clue.
new example: We will build up to the launch with a week of posts.

old definition: To happen in the period before a key event — the activities and communication that come first.
new definition: To happen in the time just before an event.
old example: In the two weeks leading up to the launch, we will post a teaser every other day to keep the audience interested.
new example: These posts lead up to the big launch day.

old definition: To mark the decreasing time before an event — often through daily posts or communications.
new definition: To count the time until an event.
old example: We are going to count down to the launch with five posts — one per day — each one revealing a new feature.
new example: We'll count down to the launch on Instagram.

old definition: To make a product or service available to users — often in stages.
new definition: To make something available step by step.
old example: We will roll out the new platform to existing clients first, then open it to new customers the following month.
new example: We will roll out the new app to clients first.

old definition: To reveal something publicly for the first time — to officially show or announce it.
new definition: To show something new to the public for the first time.
old example: At the launch event, Riley is going to unveil the new platform name and show a live demo.
new example: She will unveil the new product on stage.

old definition: To create excitement and conversation around a product or event — to get people talking before it happens.
new definition: To get many people talking about something.
old example: The teaser campaign is designed to generate buzz — we want people talking about the launch before it even happens.
new example: Our teaser videos generate buzz online.

old definition: A website or tool that helps people find information online — the most widely used is Google.
new definition: A website like Google that helps you find things online.
old example: Most of our website traffic comes from search engines — potential clients type a question into Google and find our article.
new example: Most of our visitors find us through a search engine.

old definition: A word or phrase that people type into a search engine when looking for something — used in content and SEO strategy.
new definition: A word or phrase people type when they search.
old example: We identified 'LinkedIn marketing for B2B' as a key keyword — now we make sure every relevant article includes that phrase.
new example: 'Marketing for small shops' is our main keyword.

old definition: The number of visitors that come to a website — measured in sessions, page views, or unique visitors.
new definition: The number of people who visit a website.
old example: Since we started our content strategy, our website traffic has increased by 60% — we are getting more visitors every month.
new example: Our website traffic went up by 60%.

old definition: The position of a website or page in search engine results — the higher the ranking, the more people see it.
new definition: Your position in a list of search results.
old example: Our article about LinkedIn strategy is now ranking on the first page of Google — it gets around 500 visitors a month.
new example: Our ranking is number one for this search.

old definition: When a user presses on a link — in digital marketing, clicks are measured to understand how many people act on an ad or search result.
new definition: When someone presses a link or button.
old example: The banner ad generated 1,200 clicks in its first week — each click brought a visitor to our landing page.
new example: Every click brings a new visitor to our page.

old definition: Search Engine Optimisation — the practice of improving a website's content and structure so it appears higher in search results.
new definition: Making a website easier to find on search engines.
old example: We invested in SEO for three months and our organic traffic doubled — without spending anything on paid advertising.
new example: Good SEO helps more people find our website.

old definition: A specific page on a website designed for a single goal — usually to get a visitor to fill in a form or sign up.
new definition: A web page made for one campaign or offer.
old example: Every campaign sends traffic to a dedicated landing page — it has one message and one call to action, nothing else.
new example: The ad sends people to our new landing page.

old definition: Traffic or results that come without paying for advertising — visitors who find you through search or content.
new definition: Not paid for; coming naturally from search.
old example: Our goal is to grow organic traffic — we want people to find us through search and content, not just paid ads.
new example: Our organic traffic grows a little every month.

old definition: To appear in search engine results when someone types a relevant query.
new definition: To appear in a list or place.
old example: If you write articles that answer questions your clients are asking, your website will start to show up in search results.
new example: Our page will show up in search results soon.

old definition: To bring visitors to a website — through content, ads, social media, or SEO.
new definition: To bring visitors to a website.
old example: Our LinkedIn posts drive traffic to the website — every post ends with a link to a relevant article or landing page.
new example: His posts drive traffic to our website.

old definition: To appear in search engine results for a specific keyword or phrase.
new definition: To appear high in search results for a word.
old example: We now rank for 'B2B LinkedIn marketing agency' on the first page of Google — that keyword brings us thirty leads a month.
new example: We want to rank for 'marketing agency'.

old definition: To follow a link from a search result, ad, or email to arrive at another page.
new definition: To press a link and go to another page.
old example: Only ten percent of people who see a search result click through to the website — so your title and description must be compelling.
new example: Many people click through to our pricing page.

old definition: To improve a piece of content or a web page so that search engines rank it higher for a specific term.
new definition: To change something so it works better for a keyword.
old example: We optimised the service page for the keyword 'LinkedIn management for B2B' — it now ranks on page one.
new example: We need to optimise this page for 'LinkedIn tips'.

old definition: To grow your visibility, reputation, and activity on websites and social media platforms over time.
new definition: To make your business easy to find and see online.
old example: Building an online presence takes time — but consistent content and good SEO compound over months into a significant competitive advantage.
new example: She wants to build her online presence on LinkedIn.

old definition: A list of topics or items to discuss during a meeting — shared in advance so everyone knows what to expect.
new definition: A list of topics for a meeting.
old example: Riley sent the agenda to the team the evening before the meeting — it had four items: campaign review, new brief, budget update, and next steps.
new example: The agenda has four items today.

old definition: A specific task that someone agrees to complete after a meeting — with a clear owner and deadline.
new definition: A task someone must do after a meeting.
old example: At the end of the meeting, Dana wrote down all the action points — she had two: update the content calendar and send the brief to the client.
new example: She has two action points from today's meeting.

old definition: A written record of what was discussed and decided in a meeting — including action points and who is responsible.
new definition: A written record of what people said in a meeting.
old example: Riley asked Dana to take the minutes so that everyone could review what was agreed and what needs to happen next.
new example: The minutes from Monday's meeting are on the shared drive.

old definition: To formally suggest an idea or course of action in a meeting — to put something forward for the group to consider.
new definition: To suggest an idea or plan.
old example: Riley proposed moving the launch date by one week to give the team more time to prepare the teaser content.
new example: I propose that we move the launch by one week.

old definition: To have the same opinion as someone, or to say yes to a suggestion or plan.
new definition: To have the same opinion as someone.
old example: The whole team agreed that LinkedIn would be the primary channel for the Q3 campaign.
new example: We all agree that LinkedIn is the best channel.

old definition: A short report on the current status of a project or task — shared in a meeting to keep everyone informed.
new definition: New information about something.
old example: Dana gave a quick update on the campaign results — reach was up 40% and leads had doubled compared to last month.
new example: Here is a quick update on our campaign.

old definition: A document or short explanation that gives a creative team the key information they need to do a piece of work.
new definition: A short document that explains a task.
old example: Riley wrote the brief for the new campaign — it included the target audience, the key message, the channels, and the deadline.
new example: The brief explains the audience and the message.

old definition: An action taken after a meeting to complete what was agreed — or a second meeting to check on progress.
new definition: A message you send after a meeting.
old example: Dana sent a follow-up email after the meeting with all the action points, owners, and deadlines — so nothing was forgotten.
new example: She sent a follow-up email after the meeting.

old definition: To write down what is discussed and decided during a meeting — so there is a record for everyone.
new definition: To write notes about what people say in a meeting.
old example: Can you take the minutes today? I want to make sure we have a clear record of what we agreed.
new example: Can you take the minutes today?

old definition: To finish discussing one topic and start discussing the next one on the agenda.
new definition: To start talking about the next topic.
old example: Okay — I think we have covered the campaign results. Let us move on to the next point: the new client brief.
new example: Let's move on to the next point.

old definition: To finish a meeting or a discussion — to bring it to a close.
new definition: To finish something.
old example: Let us wrap up — we only have five minutes left. Can we quickly go through the action points?
new example: Let's wrap up the meeting now.

old definition: To check on the progress of something that was agreed or discussed in a previous meeting.
new definition: To check on something again later.
old example: I will follow up on the client brief next Tuesday — by then Dana should have the first draft ready.
new example: I'll follow up on the brief next Tuesday.

old definition: To mention or introduce a topic in a meeting — to raise something for the group to discuss.
new definition: To start talking about a topic.
old example: Riley brought up the budget issue early in the meeting — she wanted everyone to know before they started planning.
new example: She wants to bring the budget problem up today.

old definition: To reach a shared decision about something — when a group comes to the same conclusion.
new definition: To decide something together.
old example: We need to agree on the launch date before we can finalise the timeline — everything depends on that date.
new example: We need to agree on the launch date.

old definition: A regularly updated page on a website where articles are published — used to share information, insights, or opinions.
new definition: A website with regular short articles.
old example: We publish two blog posts per week — one thought leadership piece and one practical how-to guide for our target audience.
new example: We post on our blog twice a week.

old definition: A written piece of content — longer and more structured than a social media post — that explores a topic in depth.
new definition: A piece of writing on a website or in a magazine.
old example: Riley wrote an article about LinkedIn strategy that was shared 200 times — it brought in 15 new leads in one week.
new example: Her article about LinkedIn got 200 shares.

old definition: A visual piece of content that presents information or data in a graphic format — easy to read and share.
new definition: A picture that shows facts with charts and icons.
old example: We turned our annual survey data into an infographic — it was much more engaging than a written report and got three times more shares.
new example: We turned our survey results into an infographic.

old definition: The technique of sharing information through a narrative or story — used to make content more memorable and emotional.
new definition: Using a story to share a message.
old example: The most effective B2B content uses storytelling — instead of listing features, it shows a real client's journey from problem to solution.
new example: Good storytelling makes people remember your brand.

old definition: The type or structure of content — for example, a video, a podcast, a written article, or an infographic.
new definition: The type of content, like video, audio or text.
old example: We tested different formats with the same audience — video performed best on LinkedIn, while long-form articles worked better in email.
new example: Video is the best format for our audience.

old definition: The specific group of people you are creating content for — defined by their job, industry, challenges, and interests.
new definition: The people who read or watch your content.
old example: All our content is created with one audience in mind — marketing managers at B2B technology companies with 50 to 500 employees.
new example: Our audience is small business owners.

old definition: The usefulness or benefit that content gives the reader — good content teaches, inspires, or solves a problem.
new definition: How useful something is to people.
old example: Every piece of content we publish must offer real value — if it does not help the reader, we do not publish it.
new example: Every post should give real value to the reader.

old definition: To share or spread content across different channels — making sure the right audience sees it.
new definition: To share content in different places.
old example: We create one strong article per week and distribute it across LinkedIn, email, and our blog — the same content reaching people in three places.
new example: We distribute each article on LinkedIn and by email.

old definition: To make a piece of content live — to post it on a website, social media platform, or other channel.
new definition: To put content online for people to see.
old example: We publish new content on LinkedIn every Tuesday and Thursday — consistency is more important than frequency.
new example: We publish content every Tuesday and Thursday.

old definition: To bring visitors to your website or landing page — often through content shared on social media or in emails.
new definition: To bring visitors to a website.
old example: A well-written article drives traffic back to your website — especially if it answers a question your audience is already searching for.
new example: This article will drive traffic to our website.

old definition: To develop a positive, reliable reputation with your audience over time — content marketing builds trust by consistently offering value.
new definition: To make people believe in you over time.
old example: Publishing useful, honest content every week builds trust with your audience — they start to see you as an expert, not just a vendor.
new example: Helpful posts build trust with our customers.

old definition: To take one piece of content and adapt it into a different format — making it work harder across more channels.
new definition: To use content again in a new form.
old example: We repurpose every blog article — we turn it into a LinkedIn post, a short video, and three social media quotes. One idea, four pieces of content.
new example: We repurpose each blog post into a short video.

old definition: A phrase or button that tells the reader what to do next — for example, 'Read the full article', 'Download our guide', or 'Book a call'.
new definition: A short line that tells people what to do next.
old example: Every piece of content needs a call to action — otherwise the reader finishes it and moves on without taking any next step.
new example: Our call to action says 'Download the guide'.

old definition: To interact with a piece of content — by liking, sharing, commenting, or clicking through to read more.
new definition: To like, comment on or share content.
old example: Our audience engages most with content that asks a question or shares a surprising statistic — it gives them a reason to comment.
new example: People engage with posts that ask a question.

old definition: The space a company occupies at a trade show — usually a table, display, and branded materials. Called a 'stand' in British English.
new definition: A small space where a company shows its products at an event.
old example: Our booth was positioned near the entrance — we chose that location to maximise the number of delegates who walked past.
new example: Our booth is near the main entrance.

old definition: A short, persuasive presentation about a company or service — designed to interest a potential client quickly.
new definition: A short talk to make someone interested in your product.
old example: Riley practised her two-minute pitch so many times that she could deliver it confidently to any type of visitor.
new example: His pitch takes only two minutes.

old definition: A printed document — like a leaflet, brochure, or case study — given to visitors at an event.
new definition: A printed page you give to people.
old example: We created a one-page handout with our top three case studies — it was easy to read and gave people a reason to remember us.
new example: Our handout shows three customer stories.

old definition: A person who attends a conference or trade show — a participant, often representing their company.
new definition: A person who goes to a conference.
old example: Over 400 delegates attended the conference — we spoke to around 60 of them at our booth over two days.
new example: Every delegate got a free coffee at our stand.

old definition: A company that has a booth or stand at a trade show — as opposed to a delegate who just attends.
new definition: A company that shows its products at an event.
old example: As an exhibitor, we paid for a premium booth position — it cost more, but the visibility was worth it.
new example: As an exhibitor, we paid for a big stand.

old definition: The activity of meeting and building professional relationships at events — exchanging contact details and starting conversations.
new definition: Meeting people to build work contacts.
old example: The evening networking session was the most valuable part of the conference — Dana made four new contacts over dinner.
new example: The evening networking session was very useful.

old definition: A potential client — someone who has shown interest but has not yet committed to buying.
new definition: A person who may become a customer.
old example: We came back from the event with twenty-five prospects — Riley followed up with every single one within 48 hours.
new example: This prospect wants a demo next week.

old definition: The action of contacting someone after a first meeting to continue the conversation and move towards a next step.
new definition: Contact you make after meeting someone.
old example: The follow-up is where most deals are won or lost — a quick, personal email within 24 hours shows professionalism and interest.
new example: Her follow-up email went out the next morning.

old definition: To deliver your short persuasive presentation — to tell someone what you do and why it matters.
new definition: To present your short sales talk.
old example: Every time a delegate stopped at our booth, Riley gave her two-minute pitch and then asked a question about their business.
new example: She is ready to give her pitch to every visitor.

old definition: To give printed documents or branded items to visitors at an event.
new definition: To give things to many people.
old example: We handed out 200 one-page case study summaries — by the end of day one, we had run out.
new example: We will hand out 200 brochures today.

old definition: To contact someone after meeting them — to continue the conversation and move towards a next step.
new definition: To contact someone again after meeting them.
old example: Riley followed up with every prospect within 48 hours of the event — a short, personal email referencing their conversation.
new example: I'll follow up with every new contact this week.

old definition: To meet someone for the first time and exchange details — to create a new professional connection.
new definition: To speak to someone for the first time.
old example: We made contact with the marketing director of a major software company — she came to our booth twice.
new example: It's easy to make contact with buyers at a trade show.

old definition: To be noticeably different and more memorable than other companies at the event.
new definition: To be easy to notice next to others.
old example: To stand out from the other exhibitors, we brought a large screen showing our client results in real time.
new example: Our gold booth helps us stand out from other exhibitors.

old definition: To gather or collect potential client contacts at an event.
new definition: To get new possible customers.
old example: We picked up thirty leads at the event — more than any other trade show we have attended this year.
new example: We hope to pick up thirty leads at the event.

old definition: Key Performance Indicator — a specific, measurable metric used to evaluate whether a goal is being achieved.
new definition: An important number that shows if you are doing well.
old example: Our three main KPIs for this campaign were: leads generated, cost per lead, and LinkedIn follower growth.
new example: Our main KPI is the number of new leads.

old definition: A measurable number used to track and assess performance — for example, clicks, reach, or conversion rate.
new definition: A number used to measure results.
old example: We track fifteen different metrics, but only three are KPIs — the ones that directly tell us whether the campaign is working.
new example: Reach is one metric we check every week.

old definition: When a visitor or lead takes the desired action — for example, signing up, booking a call, or making a purchase.
new definition: When a visitor does what you want, like buy or sign up.
old example: Our landing page had a conversion rate of eight percent — for every 100 visitors, eight filled in the contact form.
new example: Every sign-up counts as a conversion.

old definition: The specific outcome you want to achieve — the reason behind all your marketing activities.
new definition: Something you want to achieve.
old example: The goal for Q3 was to generate fifty qualified leads — we achieved sixty-two, which was twenty-four percent above target.
new example: Our goal is fifty new leads this quarter.

old definition: A specific number or result you are trying to reach — a measurable version of a goal.
new definition: A number you aim to reach.
old example: Our target was 500 LinkedIn followers by the end of the quarter — we reached 620, which was 24% above target.
new example: Our target is 500 new followers.

old definition: A standard or reference point used to compare your results — either from your past performance or industry averages.
new definition: A standard you compare your results with.
old example: The industry benchmark for email open rates in B2B is around 22% — our campaign achieved 31%, well above benchmark.
new example: Our results are above the industry benchmark.

old definition: A document or presentation that summarises what happened in a campaign — including results, insights, and next steps.
new definition: A document that shows results.
old example: Riley sent the monthly report every first Monday — it included three pages of data and a one-paragraph summary of key insights.
new example: The monthly report goes out every Monday.

old definition: A useful understanding gained from looking at data — not just the number, but what it means and what to do about it.
new definition: A useful new understanding from data.
old example: The most important insight from the data was that video content outperformed articles by 300% on LinkedIn — so we shifted our strategy.

old definition: To achieve or reach a specific numerical goal.

new example: It feels great to hit a target early.

old definition: To monitor and record a specific number over time — to watch how it changes.

new example: We track our clicks every week.

old definition: To compare your results to a standard reference point — to see if you are above or below average.
new definition: To compare results with a standard.
old example: We always measure our results against the industry benchmark — it puts our performance in context.
new example: We measure our results against the industry average.

old definition: To go above and beyond a goal — to perform better than expected.
new definition: To do better than a number you aimed for.

new example: We hope to exceed our sales target.

old definition: To not quite reach a goal — to perform below the target that was set.

old definition: To separate data into parts so it is easier to understand — to analyse in detail.

new example: Let me break down the data by channel.

old definition: A long-term plan that explains how you will achieve your goals — what you will do, why, and in what order.
new definition: A plan to reach a big goal.

new example: Our marketing strategy for next year has three priorities.

old definition: How a company presents itself relative to competitors — what makes it different and why clients should choose it.

old definition: The stages a potential client goes through from first contact to becoming a paying customer — the sales and marketing funnel.

new example: We have twenty prospects in the pipeline.

old definition: A model that describes the journey from awareness to purchase — wide at the top (many people) and narrow at the bottom (fewer who buy).

old definition: A coordinated set of marketing activities designed to achieve a specific goal over a defined period.

new example: The campaign cost €5,000, and the ROI was very high.

old definition: The combination of channels used to reach the target audience — for example, LinkedIn, email, and events.

old definition: A structured assessment of what happened — looking back at results and deciding what to change going forward.

old definition: To create and organise a plan — combining different elements into one coherent strategy.

old definition: To help a prospect progress from awareness to purchase — through content, nurturing, and sales activity.

old definition: To look back at results and assess whether the strategy worked — and what to change.

new example: We review performance every three months.

old definition: To increase the size or investment in something that is working well.
